results.title: This obscure Fedora distro eliminates the one problem that makes people abandon Linux entirely
results.author: Ayush Pande
results.content:
My first foray down the Linux rabbit hole was with the Raspberry Pi OS (or rather, Raspbian Buster, as it was called back then) ages ago on my first RPi board. Since then, I’ve tried all sorts of Linux flavors, including wacky distributions and meme-worthy options. But I have to admit that despite most mainstream Linux distros becoming more beginner-friendly, they tend to have their fair share of problems.
For one, stability can be a real problem on conventional distributions, and even with all the safeguards in modern Linux flavors, you could still end up bricking your OS with the wrong command. Fortunately, distros like Fedora Silverblue can tackle this reliability problem, and while I wouldn’t go so far as to say they’re superior to conventional Linux options in every way, they definitely have some perks for folks looking for a stable, general-purpose OS for their daily driver.
Troubleshooting broken packages can be painful when you’re just starting out
Especially since updates can introduce faulty packages or broken dependencies
Let’s say you went with an Ubuntu installation for your everyday machine. While it’s one of the easier distros to pick up and use, you could still end up with broken packages if you’re not careful. Since the system files are fully accessible to the root user, accidentally running an rm command for the wrong system folder or tweaking certain config files can render your machine unusable.
The core OS package updates on Linux are typically more stable than the buggy mess that Windows 11 often ships, but that doesn’t mean you won’t encounter the occasional broken package on the former. Unless you’ve got a proper backup pipeline, you might have some trouble recovering your PC if a faulty update messes up the core files. And that’s before I talk about all the shenanigans caused by malware. Of course, you can still look into different ways to troubleshoot these problems, but distros like Silverblue can bypass them altogether.
Fedora Silverblue adds an extra layer of stability to your setup
And it’s all thanks to its immutable design
Unlike typical Linux distributions, Silverblue is an immutable OS, meaning the core system files are locked in a read-only mode. Essentially, typical commands or packages can’t edit your root files. Since this also applies to user-run commands and custom scripts, you don’t have to worry about accidentally breaking your Linux PC when you’re still figuring things out as a newcomer.
The update mechanism in Silverblue also counters faulty package update issues. Unlike typical distros (including good ol’ Fedora Workstation), the core packages get updated one-by-one while the host OS is still running in the background. If things go wrong and you don’t have any snapshots/backups, you can’t roll back to a stable state. Meanwhile, the base OS packages in Silverblue get downloaded as new bootable system images, which are then applied at the start of the next boot cycle. If things go south during the update process, you can just discard the new image and proceed with the old one, making the entire recovery process a cakewalk.
As you may have guessed, Silverblue can’t really install apps via conventional package managers, and instead requires different workarounds for custom software. The GNOME desktop environment has a Software Center utility that’s capable of installing full-on GUI apps as flatpaks. For the uninitiated, flakpaks are containerized environments that can run entire apps without letting them interfere with the base OS packages, and you can update them via this easy-to-access app marketplace.
But personally, I rely a lot on the rpm-ostree hybrid image system, which can install traditional RPM packages on top of the base image. Unlike the flatpaks on Software Center, many of the packages within rpm-ostree let me configure essential CLI tools for my Silverblue machine. And for apps that are available in neither utility, good ol’ Distrobox can run them as containers via the Podman/Docker runtimes.
That said, Silverblue has some quirks as well
As much as I adore Silverblue, I can’t end this article without discussing some of its flaws. Its immutable design may make it more stable and foolproof, but it also doesn’t support the full range of customization options as typical Linux flavors. Sure, rpm-ostree lets you load GNOME tweaks to tinker with certain appearance settings, but you can’t fine-tune every aspect of the distro.
Although Silverblue’s stable experience is definitely useful for newcomers who just want to get out of Windows’ bloat-riddled walled garden, you won’t be able to mess around with the system files, configs, and core packages on this immutable OS the same way you could on traditional Linux distros.
results.summary:
Fedora Silverblue offers a highly stable, immutable Linux experience that prevents system-breaking errors by locking core files and allowing users to easily roll back failed software updates.

### Key Points
- Fedora Silverblue utilizes an immutable design that keeps core system files in a read-only state to prevent accidental user-driven damage.
- The operating system updates by downloading new bootable images, allowing users to revert to a previous state if an update fails.
- Software management relies on Flatpaks for containerized GUI applications and rpm-ostree for installing traditional RPM packages.
- Distrobox allows users to run additional software within containers using Podman or Docker runtimes.
- The immutable architecture limits deep system customization compared to traditional, mutable Linux distributions.

### Why it Matters
This immutable approach provides a more reliable computing environment for Linux newcomers by eliminating the risk of bricking the OS through faulty commands or broken dependencies. It represents a shift toward more resilient desktop operating systems that prioritize system integrity and simplified recovery over unrestricted file-system access.

results.title: OpenAI engineer arrested in bugging of executive conference room
results.author: George Kelly, Michael McLaughlin
results.content:
An OpenAI engineer has been arrested on suspicion of hiding an audio recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco headquarters, federal prosecutors said Tuesday.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Friday and charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He made his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday and remains in custody.
An unattended bag found in the company’s offices contained Alfozan’s wallet and identification, as well as a second recording device, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in San Francisco.
Alfozan has worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors said. He has been a legal permanent resident of the U.S. since Sept. 2020, court documents said.
OpenAI personnel found the device Sept. 30. It was plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room and had been concealed in toilet paper, the complaint says. The company determined it was installed around Sept. 28, and its contents were encrypted.
Surveillance footage shows Alfozan near the room on multiple dates before the discovery, though he was not authorized to enter the room or attend meetings there, prosecutors said. Meetings in the room frequently involved confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and government engagements, according to the complaint.
Before the device was installed, Alfozan used a productivity tool to ask about OpenAI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, room capacities, and calendars, as well as the locations of leadership and outside partner meetings, the complaint alleges.
A chatbot account tied to Alfozan’s spouse, which shared identifiers with his own account, submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 about building, installing, obscuring, and remotely accessing a recording device, prosecutors said. Queries included how to “build a continuous audio recorder” and “encrypt the SD card,” prosecutors claimed. On Sept. 27 and 28, the account asked about the specific device that was later found, including its unique MAC address.
“For us it is a matter of national security,” U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian said in a statement.
On Oct. 5, the complaint says, Alfozan entered the conference room and appeared to look behind the television. That same day, he allegedly left a bag unattended in a printer. Security personnel who opened it found his wallet and ID, along with a second recording device similar to the first. He later reported that he’d misplaced the bag to company officials.
OpenAI examined the device in the bag, which had a recording microcontroller and had been customized to obfuscate stored data, “such as potentially intercepted audio communications,” according to an FBI affidavit.
When Alfozan retrieved the bag on Oct. 6, it no longer contained the device. He reported that his credit card, approximately $500, two AirPods, headphones, sunglasses and a power bank were stolen, but made no mention of the recording device, the affidavit said.
FBI Director Kash Patel said protecting U.S. AI innovation is among the bureau’s highest counterintelligence priorities. Scott Schelble, special agent in charge of the FBI’s San Francisco field office, said the agency is committed to protecting sensitive research and proprietary technology.
If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release.
The case is being prosecuted by the National Security, Cyber & Special Prosecutions Section of the U.S. attorney’s office for the Northern District of California.
OpenAI said on X (opens in new tab) that after discovering the device, employees used the company’s AI models to determine what it was and where it came from, and referred the matter to the FBI. The company thanked the agents and prosecutors who “moved quickly to make an arrest.”
According to OpenAI, its technical surveillance countermeasures team found the device during a sweep of a conference room.
OpenAI described the device as sophisticated and designed to evade detection, saying it had advanced encryption, audio monitoring capabilities, and a mechanism for transferring data in a way meant to avoid monitoring. The company said investigators used its models to analyze forensic images of the device’s storage and assess changes in the underlying data.
Court documents filed by prosecutors identified the recording device as Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, a thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage. Amazon sells it for $23.99.
The company said it has evidence that Alfozan intended to place other recording devices in sensitive spaces to secretly record meetings.
According to OpenAI, Alfozan was a member of the product team. The company said it coordinated the timing of his firing with the FBI to avoid disrupting the investigation, and he was terminated Friday, the day he was arrested. Between Sept. 30 and that date, OpenAI said, it gradually restricted his access to systems and spaces, then suspended his physical and network access, placed him on leave, and secured his company-issued equipment.
A YouTube video last month touted him as the only Saudi employee at OpenAI.
“Honestly, this one year felt like five years anywhere else,” he said in response to a question about his experience.
“The idea of AI is that it handles things one might not want to do, so they can focus on tasks or hobbies they enjoy more or work they take pleasure in and let it do the tedious tasks,” Alfozan said later in the video.
A LinkedIn profile that matches Alfozan’s name lists his OpenAI role as engineering lead on the company’s AI agents platform.
The resume said he has been a venture partner with Riyadh-based RAED Ventures since 2025. The company did not respond to The Standard’s inquiries.
Before joining OpenAI, he was a founding engineer at Nash, an AI infrastructure company for logistics, from 2022 to August 2025, according to the LinkedIn profile.
From 2017 to 2022, he was a senior systems engineer at Meta. His earlier experience, according to the profile, includes a stint as a systems engineer at Reach Labs, a wireless power startup in Y Combinator’s summer 2015 batch, and internships at Microsoft, SAP in Berlin and Akamai Technologies.
He has a master’s degree in data science from UC Berkeley, the LinkedIn profile says.
A man in the passenger seat of a car at Alfozan’s Millbrae home said that the family did not want to speak to reporters.
OpenAI said it has no indication that Alfozan improperly accessed or took model weights, source code, or customer data and has not seen activity that compromised the safety of its products or customers’ information. The company said it will continue to support the FBI’s investigation.
OpenAI said it treats protecting its technology, data and people “as a matter of national importance” and called the case an example of how AI can counter sophisticated security threats.
A detention hearing before U.S. Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse is set for Oct. 19.
More about the authors
Michael is a deputy breaking news editor at The Standard.
results.summary:
Federal prosecutors have charged OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan with attempting to intercept oral communications after he allegedly planted a recording device in a San Francisco executive conference room.

### Key Points
- Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old OpenAI engineer, was arrested Friday and charged with attempting to intercept oral communications.
- Investigators discovered a concealed recording device plugged into a television in an executive conference room on September 30.
- Prosecutors allege Alfozan used productivity tools and chatbot prompts to research how to build, hide, and remotely access the recording hardware.
- Surveillance footage reportedly shows Alfozan entering unauthorized areas, and a second recording device was later found in a bag he left unattended.
- OpenAI stated that no model weights, source code, or customer data were compromised during the incident.
- If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

### Why it Matters
This case highlights the growing national security concerns surrounding the protection of proprietary artificial intelligence research and sensitive corporate strategy. It underscores the critical need for robust internal security measures as tech companies increasingly become targets for industrial espionage and intellectual property theft.

results.title: Iran threatens Gulf data centres: How exposed is the region’s internet?
results.author: Nils Adler
results.content:
Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, has warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence (AI) facilities across the region could be attacked if war with the United States erupts again.
The warning comes as the capture of Yemeni territory along the Red Sea coastline last month by the Iran-backed Houthis has raised concerns over the safety of internet cables linking Europe and Asia. Fierce fighting is under way between Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis at several locations, including Bab al-Mandeb, through which nearly one-fifth of global internet traffic passes.
Data centres and US business interests were hit in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates during the US-Israel war on Iran. Tehran said these attacks were in response to US attacks on Iranian civilian installations.
Active hostilities have largely ended since the June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US, but attacks on ships passing through the global oil chokepoint – the Strait of Hormuz – have continued.
So how exposed is the region’s internet? Here’s what you need to know:
Why are data centres and internet cables vulnerable?
Because so much data travels through a few narrow routes.
More than 90 percent of data capacity between Europe and Asia passes through cables under the Red Sea, according to estimates by the research firm TeleGeography.
They enter the sea through Bab al-Mandeb, a strait about 26km (16 miles) wide at its narrowest, one of the busiest maritime routes connecting Europe to Asia.
Cables can be cut by anchors or sabotage, and repairs in a war zone need permits and safety guarantees.
Data centres, which run banking apps and cloud services, are large, fixed targets.
“An attack does not necessarily need to destroy the servers themselves to render an entire facility inoperable,” Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
Data centres depend on uninterrupted electricity, cooling and telecommunications, he said, while undersea cables “are difficult to protect continuously and disruption can affect several countries simultaneously”.
Has Iran threatened to attack data centres and cables?
Yes, repeatedly since the war began in February.
On March 11, the semi-official Tasnim news agency said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has published a list of “Iran’s new targets”, including cloud infrastructure belonging to Google, Microsoft and Oracle in Israel and some Gulf states.
That same month, the IRGC named 17 US firms in a Telegram post, including Google, Meta, and Apple, as well as the Emirati AI company G42 as potential targets.
Krieg said he would take Rezaei’s threat seriously, but drew a distinction between Iran’s ability to cause significant disruption and its ability “to systematically destroy the Gulf’s digital infrastructure”.
“What makes Mohsen Rezaei’s warning particularly significant is that he is not simply threatening another set of targets,” he said. “He is identifying a new category of strategic infrastructure that connects Gulf economic diversification directly to American technological power.”
He described the warning as “fundamentally about deterrence”, aimed “as much at Abu Dhabi, Riyadh and Doha as at Washington”, giving Gulf governments a reason to discourage another US offensive.
Have tech infrastructure and cables been attacked before?
Yes.
In March, Amazon Web Services (AWS) said two of its facilities in the UAE were “directly struck” by drones, while a strike near one in Bahrain “caused physical impact to our infrastructure”.
Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank said its app was unavailable due to a region-wide IT disruption, though it did not directly link this to AWS.
In September, AWS said it could not restore several sites in Bahrain and one in the UAE.
Under the sea, three cables were damaged in February 2024, most likely by the dragging anchor of the Rubymar, a cargo ship disabled by a Houthi missile, according to the industry consensus reported by Data Center Dynamics, with repairs taking months.
In September 2025, two cables were cut near Jeddah, slowing internet access across the Middle East and South Asia. No cause has been confirmed.
The March attacks “exposed the limits of treating commercial infrastructure as something that automatically benefits from national air defence”, Krieg said.
“Gulf militaries can intercept most incoming threats, but even a small number of successful strikes can produce disproportionate economic consequences,” he said, adding that relatively cheap drones can threaten facilities holding billions of dollars’ worth of equipment.
Have the Houthis attacked undersea cables?
Not directly, as far as is known, and the group has denied causing the 2024 damage.
But in mid-September, the Houthis seized the port of Mocha and territory around Bab al-Mandeb.
On September 11, they reached Mayyun Island, which splits the strait in two.
On October 5, Yemen’s internationally recognised government said it had retaken Mocha and positions near the strait. The Houthis denied it.
Are there alternatives to the Red Sea?
Some, but they cost more and are still being built.
On September 10, Iraq signed a contract with Qatar’s Ooredoo to carry data from the Gulf to Europe across its territory, the Ministry of Communications said in a statement.
Minister Mustafa Jabar Sanad told the Iraqi News Agency the underground cable runs from al-Faw to Rabia near Turkiye’s border.
On October 7, Ooredoo’s international arm agreed to buy fibre from Iraq’s iQ Networks to extend the route towards Turkiye, subject to government approval.
Microsoft said in September it would invest more than $400m in subsea and land connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, in a blog post.
The technology news site Rest of World reported on October 7, citing an unnamed source, that Google and Meta had begun sending some traffic through Iraq.
Neither company has responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Krieg said genuine resilience would require geographical redundancy, “potentially including facilities outside the Gulf”.
“That creates a tension between digital sovereignty and operational security,” he said, as Gulf governments have invested heavily in keeping sensitive data and computing within their own borders.
How will it affect the Gulf’s tech hub ambitions?
Investment continues, but the war has already taken a toll on the sector. Gulf states have staked their post-oil economies on technology.
In Abu Dhabi, the Emirati firm G42 is building Stargate UAE with OpenAI, Nvidia and others.
It sits within a planned 5-gigawatt UAE-US AI campus.
Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund launched Humain, an AI company chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in May 2025 to build data centres and an Arabic-language AI model, the Saudi Press Agency reported.
Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund joined the US investor Blue Owl in a $3bn data centre push in September 2025.
In September, Microsoft said it would invest more than $10bn in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE through 2030, with a new focus on “digital resilience”, in a blog post.
But AWS said it had “exhausted every option” to restore some data hosted in Bahrain.
Krieg said the threats would not “fundamentally reverse” Gulf ambitions, but would “change the economics and geography of AI investment”.
“The Gulf has traditionally sold itself as a stable environment in an unstable region. The war has challenged that proposition,” he said.
The UAE is particularly exposed, he said, because its AI strategy is “deeply integrated with American technology companies”, making Emirati infrastructure “more attractive as a target for Iran”. Qatar, with its diplomatic ties to Tehran, is “somewhat better positioned politically”.
“In many ways, Iran is threatening to do to the Gulf’s emerging digital economy what it has already done to its maritime economy,” Krieg said – to “make reliability itself a geopolitical bargaining chip”.
results.summary:
Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei has warned that regional data centers and undersea internet cables could face attacks if hostilities between Iran and the United States escalate further.

### Key Points
- Over 90 percent of data capacity between Europe and Asia relies on undersea cables passing through the narrow Bab al-Mandeb strait.
- The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has identified cloud infrastructure belonging to major firms like Google, Microsoft, and Oracle as potential targets.
- Amazon Web Services reported physical damage to facilities in the UAE and Bahrain following drone strikes earlier this year.
- Cargo ship incidents and regional conflict have previously caused significant undersea cable disruptions, impacting internet connectivity across the Middle East and South Asia.
- Gulf nations are currently pursuing alternative land-based data routes through Iraq to reduce reliance on vulnerable maritime infrastructure.

### Why it Matters
These threats jeopardize the ambitious digital transformation strategies of Gulf states that rely on deep integration with American technology companies. By targeting critical infrastructure, Iran is effectively turning regional economic stability into a geopolitical bargaining chip in its ongoing standoff with the United States.

results.title: Ledger Confirms Spy Chip Implant Behind Wallet Crypto Thefts
results.author: BeauHD
results.content:
Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from BleepingComputer: Ledger has confirmed that some of its devices distributed through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis were compromised with a hardware implant that drained users' cryptocurrency wallets. The company has been investigating reports of users losing funds from wallets purchased through CryptoBilis, a major Malaysia-based hardware wallet retailer operating across Southeast Asia. Some researchers have shown the implant in Ledger X since September 16, saying tampered devices were available for nearly half the price of the original hardware.
[...] In a report over the weekend, Tibane Labs notes that the threat actor made room for the malicious circuitry by replacing the original battery with a smaller one, which powers both the implant and the Ledger X. "Under the battery and antenna sits an ST STM32G431KBU6 (Arm CortexM4, 128 KB flash, UFQFPN32)," the researchers found inside one of the devices. For connectivity, the actor used "a tiny eSIM, an 8pad package just 2x2 mm, next to the MCU, and a shielded LTE module that sends the words out."
[...] Ledger is advising users to avoid purchasing from unauthorized resellers as they run an increased risk of getting counterfeit or modified devices. The company is also reminding its authorized resellers and distributors to get the products only through authorized channels and to avoid restocking returned products. Ledger provides a 'Genuine Check' mechanism to determine the authenticity of the device; however, it explicitly warns that it cannot detect added implants when the device's original Secure Element remains intact.
results.summary:
Ledger has confirmed that hardware wallets sold by the Malaysian reseller CryptoBilis were compromised with malicious implants designed to steal cryptocurrency by transmitting private keys via cellular networks.

### Key Points
- Ledger identified tampered Ledger X devices distributed through the Southeast Asian retailer CryptoBilis.
- Attackers replaced original batteries with smaller versions to accommodate malicious circuitry, including an Arm Cortex-M4 microcontroller and an LTE module.
- The implants exfiltrate sensitive wallet data using a tiny eSIM, allowing unauthorized parties to drain user funds.
- Ledger warns that its "Genuine Check" feature cannot detect these hardware modifications if the device's original Secure Element remains intact.
- The company advises customers to purchase hardware wallets exclusively through authorized channels to avoid counterfeit or modified products.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights a critical supply chain vulnerability where physical tampering can bypass standard digital security verification methods. It serves as a stark reminder for users to prioritize purchasing security hardware directly from manufacturers to mitigate the risk of sophisticated, hardware-level fraud.

results.title: Rivian spinoff Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
results.author: Andrew J. Hawkins
results.content:
Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO’s secretive robotics project.
Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
Ford’s former EV and software chief will run Rivian’s robotics startup at a time of maximum hype for physical AI.
Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company’s ultimately unsuccessful Project Titan effort to make an autonomous electric car. He had a previous stint at Apple as VP of Mac hardware engineering, but he left the company in 2013 to become Tesla’s chief vehicle engineer, where he helped oversee the Model 3 sedan. He left Tesla in 2018 and rejoined Apple. In 2021, Field was hired by Ford to run the automaker’s electric vehicle and software division, a position he held until earlier this year.
Mind Robotics said Field will oversee its effort to build “universally capable robots” for the purpose of working in Rivian’s factories, as well as other applications. The startup was founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe in 2025, and has since raised over $1 billion in financing. While the company has yet to show off any of its robots in public, the startup says its robots are being designed with “dexterity and physical reasoning” that’s required for industrial work.
“Doug is a remarkable leader with a track record of delivering new technologies in successful products, and I couldn’t be more excited to be building Mind with him,” Scaringe said in a statement. “He has an incredible ability to foster great teams that take on big, complex ideas and deliver products that reset expectations. That’s exactly what Mind needs as we deploy robots into real factories and beyond.”
Field joins Mind Robotics at a major turning point for the field of robotics, with rapid advances in physical AI colliding with major hurdles in hardware and software development. Several companies, like Tesla and Hyundai, are pursuing humanoid robots for factory and warehouse work — even as experts note that making a robot act like a human is easier than scaling the technology for practical work. Mind Robotics hasn’t confirmed whether it’s working on a humanoid design or something else entirely. The company has been on a hiring spree and currently has 32 open positions.
Scaringe, who serves as acting CEO and chair of Mind Robotics, has said he wants to keep the companies separate, rather than try to combine the work like Tesla. That said, the companies are certainly linked in several ways. Mind Robotics is using AI training data from Rivian, and the robots will be initially tested in Rivian’s factories. Rivian also owns equity in Mind Robotics and will be the first customer for its robots.
Field said he is excited for the challenge in running the new startup.
“Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important—and difficult—engineering challenges of our time,” he said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.”
Correction October 13th: Mind Robotics is a partner of Rivian, but not a spinoff. A previous version of this story misstated the relationship between the companies.
results.summary:
Mind Robotics, a secretive startup founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe, has appointed former Ford and Apple executive Doug Field as its new president to lead robotics development.

### Key Points
- Doug Field, formerly a top executive at Ford, Tesla, and Apple, will lead Mind Robotics as its new president.
- Founded by RJ Scaringe in 2025, Mind Robotics has secured over $1 billion in financing to develop universally capable industrial robots.
- The startup plans to utilize AI training data from Rivian and test its initial robotic hardware within Rivian’s high-volume manufacturing facilities.
- Mind Robotics is currently expanding its workforce with 32 open positions to accelerate the development of robots featuring advanced dexterity and physical reasoning.
- While competitors like Tesla and Hyundai are pursuing humanoid designs, Mind Robotics has not yet disclosed the specific form factor of its technology.

### Why it Matters
This appointment signals a significant push to integrate advanced physical AI into industrial manufacturing environments. By leveraging Rivian’s factory data and infrastructure, the company aims to overcome the scaling challenges that have historically hindered the widespread adoption of autonomous robotics.

results.title: AI labs are fueling a wild market for your Slack DMs
results.author: Charles Rollet,Tom Carter,Stephen Council
results.content:
As they race to automate white-collar work, AI labs have found the perfect source of training data: your Slack DMs.
Business owners are getting six-figure "exploding offers" that expire in 48 hours to sell their data. Instagram is flooded with ads declaring that "AI needs your data" and promising millions. The data is priced by the terabyte, anonymized, and sold to AI giants desperate for an edge.
Tech giants have moved to harvest their employees' data for AI training. And, once focused on dead startups, brokers now pay for live data from active companies.
"Right now, the demand is just astronomical," said Dan Novaes, the CEO of Mode.Inc, a startup that sells data to AI model developers.
Mundane workplace data is more valuable than ever as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others build AI agents for businesses. Annual spending on data for AI is projected to explode from less than $1 billion last year to almost $6.5 billion in 2027, Gartner estimates.
The boom has a darker side. Employees rarely profit from — or know about — their Slacks, PowerPoints, and Google Docs being sold to the highest bidder. Suspected hackers have shopped around a large company's stolen codebase for millions of dollars. Meta's attempt to harvest its own employees' data for its AI models sparked a revolt.
Some CEOs are getting blindsided. Doug Kreuzkamp, who runs airline operations company Springshot, was sitting in his office on a Zoom call in August when he found out that Google had bought his data. Springshot, a longtime vendor for the now-bankrupt Spirit Airlines, helped flights coordinate with workers such as gate agents and cleaners.
"I had less than 48 hours' notice — from the media — that the intellectual property we had spent 15 years building could be given away," Kreuzkamp told Business Insider.
The surging market is pushing into uncharted waters, and the industry risks a reckoning with workers and regulators, said Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University. The lack of federal privacy laws leaves few legal barriers to companies collecting data from their employees for AI training, she added.
"The question is, does the consent of the employees from whom they collected that data actually extend to the sale of the data? I think it's an ethically gray area," Ajunwa said.
Business data has become the new oil
The boom has created a thriving group of go-betweens who hunt for small businesses rich in data and low on cash. After scrubbing sensitive information like Social Security numbers and home addresses, they resell it to AI giants.
Although the industry is new, it's become highly competitive. Ryan Lock, cofounder of AI broker Polyshares, compares it to the oil boom that hit Texas in the early 1900s, when prospectors snapped up cheap land from farmers who didn't realize the true value of the oil underneath it.
Small-business owners sitting on troves of internal records may not realize the seemingly mundane files could be worth big money. Tactics like 48-hour deadlines have become common, Lock said.
"The offers being made look almost identical to those early oil offers," he said from his home base in Dallas. "They'll say, 'I'm offering you double market. I need an answer by Friday.'"
Lock and his cofounders went through the data-licensing process themselves with their other companies, sometimes laughing out loud at the lowball offers they got. Their firm tries to bridge that information gap by giving business owners more transparency about what their data is worth.
"There's still plenty of money for everyone, but business owners should receive more of the benefit," he said.
Wanted: data from companies, dead or alive
Data that demonstrates how work is actually done is highly valuable, said William Almeida, the chief revenue officer of AI training startup Micro1, because it provides critical context on how decisions are made and products are built.
That information can help train agents, the autonomous computer-using AI tools that have become a major focus for companies like Meta and SpaceXAI. As AI companies build new models, the real-world data guides the AI on how best to handle specific tasks.
Micro1 announced a program earlier this year that pays midsize companies $100,000 to $2 million for access to anonymized data. Almeida said AI developers increasingly want "long-horizon" data that can provide a full picture of how work gets done. If a company won't sell its Slack, customer relationship management, or email records, the rest of the corpus is less valuable.
The data is priced based on a multitude of factors, with volume being a critical one. The more white-collar employees a company has, the more valuable its data corpus is, said Novaes, the Mode.Inc CEO.
Other factors, like exclusivity, matter — there's lower demand for a codebase that a rival lab already has its hands on. Fields that AI giants are trying the hardest to automate, like law and accounting, see especially high demand.
Generally, though, any company — dead or alive, big or small — can sell its data, as long as it has enough.
"People need to wake up to it and take this opportunity," Novaes said.
Grant Gooley decided to license his company's data to an AI training company. His agency, MyPortal Marketing, has sold Micro1 everything from Figma and Canva files to checklists for onboarding clients to Google ads. He said it didn't sell client-specific material.
"If AI is going to be trained, why not be part of that, and do it responsibly?" Gooley said.
A new breed of security and privacy concerns
While the market creates wealth for some, it's breeding new kinds of cybersecurity and privacy risks for others.
Nick Heiner helps improve AI agents by building office-like digital environments at AI training startup Surge AI. Heiner said that earlier this year, he was approached by a group offering a large company's codebase for millions of dollars.
"It became apparent that this group did not have the rights to sell this data," Heiner told Business Insider. "They had illicitly obtained a copy of the codebase and were just going around to all the data vendors saying, 'Can I get a few million bucks for this?'"
Security and consent concerns aren't limited to hackers. Google's bid to buy Spirit Airlines' old data for $10 million has been held up, in part, by flight attendants worried about how their records will be used. Last week, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and over 100 other members of Congress wrote a letter to Google and Spirit urging the companies to protect the privacy of thousands of former Spirit employees.
A Google spokesperson told Business Insider that it's not looking to buy any personal information from Spirit Airlines and that any such data would be either excluded or de-identified by an independent third party. A representative for Spirit said the company is working closely with the flight attendants and other unions to address their concerns.
Former gig workers for Mercor, another AI training startup, have alleged in an ongoing lawsuit that the company encouraged them to upload work materials without their employers' consent. Mercor has denied their claims in court.
The hunger for work records is so strong that some tech giants have tried tracking their own staff.
At Meta, employees revolted when the company announced a new program earlier this year to track their keystrokes and mouse movements for AI training. Employees worried that Meta would capture their sensitive data, like credit card numbers and immigration documents.
Although Meta's chief technology officer, Andrew Bosworth, pledged that the data would be "tightly controlled," it turned out that it had been viewable across the company in a major internal leak. The supposedly anonymized data included employees' private conversations and performance records, screenshots obtained by Business Insider show. Meta suspended the project shortly after the breach and hasn't restarted it.
Google once considered tracking its staff's AI output and ultimately dropped the idea, Business Insider previously reported.
The Meta revolt hasn't stopped other companies from eyeing employee data as a useful shortcut to AI domination, including the world's richest man.
In an all-hands meeting in August, CEO Elon Musk told employees that SpaceX would train its Grok AI on worker data and encouraged them to think of themselves as the model's "parents."
"In a way, it will be trained on you. It will inherit your thoughts and ideas and beliefs, and I think that's a good thing," Musk said.
A huge market that few workers are aware of
Though the company data market is nascent, the AI training startups cashing in are optimistic.
Ali Ansari, Micro1's CEO, says licensing data to labs could become one of the most common revenue sources for businesses worldwide, he recently posted on X. He estimates that, soon, about 10% of the US's GDP could be dedicated to training AI models, thanks to business data and human professionals.
Last week, Micro1 announced a commitment to spend $1 billion on company data over the next 12 months.
The growing use of employee records for AI training could heighten the urgency of calls for new data protection and privacy regulations, said Alex Rosenblat, a sociologist and former Uber policy executive.
It could also give employees new leverage and negotiating power as the value of their everyday digital footprint grows, she said.
"It's not that data collection wasn't present before; it's that the scale at which it can happen, the scale at which it is useful, has shifted," Rosenblat said.
"And that's an opportunity for people to say, 'wait a minute, the value of this is escaping us.'"
results.summary:
AI labs are aggressively purchasing internal business data, including Slack messages and documents, to train autonomous AI agents, creating a booming but controversial market for workplace information.

### Key Points
- Annual spending on data for AI training is projected to grow from under $1 billion in 2023 to nearly $6.5 billion by 2027.
- Startups like Micro1 are offering businesses between $100,000 and $2 million to license anonymized internal records for model development.
- Tech giants including Meta and SpaceX have faced internal backlash for attempting to harvest employee keystrokes and communications for AI training.
- Data brokers are using high-pressure tactics, such as 48-hour "exploding offers," to acquire proprietary information from small and midsize companies.
- The lack of federal privacy laws has created an ethically gray area regarding whether employee consent is required for the sale of workplace data.

### Why it Matters
The commodification of internal business records transforms mundane workplace communications into a high-value asset, potentially creating a new, significant revenue stream for companies. However, this trend raises urgent questions about employee privacy, intellectual property rights, and the potential for security breaches when sensitive corporate data is sold to third-party developers.

results.title: All about the new Apple HomeView smart home device
results.author: Ankur Thakur
results.content:
Apple has launched a new device called the “HomeView,” which is a smart home hub with a 7-inch square touchscreen display, FaceTime camera, speakers, and microphones.
It’s a fusion of a HomePod (on the speaker side) and an iPad (on the display side), meant to sit on a desk or tabletop, or be mounted to the wall.
You can use it to ask Siri all sorts of questions, control your Home, view CCTV camera feeds, make FaceTime calls, listen to music, see recipes on the screen, access your messages or have it read to you, reply to messages using voice or on-screen keyboard, use it as an Intercom machine to broadcast to other devices in your house, and more.
Just as HomePod can recognize different family members by voice, the new HomeView can recognize up to 6 users by face (using the front camera; HomeView doesn’t have Face ID). Based on this recognition, it can show personalized responses for that person in Siri, Messages, Calendar, Reminders, FaceTime, and Find My.
Here’s a quick summary of what you need to know about it.
Types
HomeView comes in two flavors:
- One has a speaker base that’s meant to sit on your desk or tabletop.
- The other is wall-mounted, which you can DIY-install or have a professional install it on your wall.
Fine print on Apple’s website says this about the wall-mounted version:
“HomeView (Wall Mounted) will be available with a choice of three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home. Power Mount USB‑C Wall Connector, available starting at $59.95 (U.S.), and Power Mount AC Wired, available starting at $79.95 (U.S.), can be ordered starting today from apple.com/store and in the Apple Store app. Power Mount PoE Wired will be available starting in early 2027 for $129.95 (U.S.).”
I’m sure that within a few weeks of launch, you’ll be able to find third-party mounts on Amazon for far less.
Colors
Apple HomeView comes in 4 colors: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray.
The wall-mounted version comes in just 2 colors: space gray and silver.
Price
Both the normal and wall-mounted versions cost $299 in the United States, $429 in Canada, A$449 in Australia, £299 in the United Kingdom, and ₹39900 in India.
The wall mount will cost more overall because you’ll need to buy the mounts, cable, and adapter separately (more in the next section).
What you get in the HomeView box
Apple’s pre-order page says the tabletop version comes with a color-matched USB-C cable and a 30-watt adapter.
However, the wall-mounted version doesn’t include any of these, even though it costs the same. You’ll have to buy mounts and adapters separately.
Construction
HomeView is made of aluminum, and the display connects to the domed speaker base with a stainless steel hinge. The hinge allows smooth tilting, so you can view it comfortably whether sitting or standing.
Weight
The desk version weighs 2.1 pounds (952 grams). The wall-mounted version weighs just 0.63 pounds (286 grams) because it lacks the large bottom speaker setup.
Dimensions
See the image above for its size.
- Left to right: 5.73 inches (14.55 cm)
- Top to bottom: 5.38–6.82 inches (13.67–17.32 cm)
Display
Apple HomeView has a 7-inch diagonal Liquid Retina IPS technology multi-touch display with 1088-by-1088-pixel resolution at 220 ppi. The display supports True Tone, has a fingerprint-resistant oleophobic coating, and reaches up to 500 nits of maximum brightness (the same as a MacBook Air display) and 0.3 nits of minimum brightness so that it isn’t too bright when you use it as a desk clock in your bedroom at night.
Smart software
Apple says that:
“The HomeView interface intelligently adjusts based on the user’s distance, showing simpler information that’s viewable from across the room and richer detail as they step closer.”
Faces
Like Apple Watch and iPad widgets, you can customize the HomeView screen with faces that show the time, calendar, photos, weather, and more.
Camera
This smart home hub device has a 12MP Center Stage camera at the top for FaceTime calls. The camera has an ƒ/2.4 aperture.
Speakers
The desk version of HomeView has:
- Two custom full-range drivers
- Custom down-firing woofer
- Dual force-canceling passive radiators
The wall-mounted version has only two custom full-range drivers, with no woofers or passive radiators. But Apple tuned it specifically for on-wall placement, so it still sounds decent with less hardware (this is what Apple claims).
Microphone
Apple HomeView has four microphones for far-field Siri, so it can hear you better when you a question or are on a FaceTime call. Here are their placements:
- Front microphone (near the camera)
- Rear microphone (on the backside at the top)
- Left and Right microphones (on the sides)
These microphones also support the Sound Recognition feature, so the device can listen for smoke and carbon monoxide alarm sounds and alert you.
Sensors
HomeView has an ambient light sensor (the same one found on phones, tablets, and laptops), so it can automatically adjust screen brightness based on the surrounding light.
It also has a temperature and humidity sensor, so you can get data for the room your HomeView is in.
Finally, it has an accelerometer for some neat features that aren’t publicly known yet.
Chip
HomeView is powered by an Apple A18 chip, which is the same chip found in iPhone 16, 16 Plus, and 16e.
Wireless tech
Apple says the HomeView hub supports Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) with MIMO9, simultaneous dual-band, peer-to-peer discovery for easy guest access, Thread networking technology, and Bluetooth 6.0.
Handoff
Like HomePod, you can bring your iPhone near your HomeView, and it will hand off music or podcasts from your mobile to this home hub. Apple says:
“With Handoff, users can continue listening to a song they were playing in the car or on a walk by placing their iPhone in front of the HomeView display.”
Multi-setup
Apple further says that:
“By setting up multiple HomeView, HomePod, HomePod mini, and AirPlay-compatible speakers around the house, users can enjoy music throughout the entire home with multiroom audio.”
Power Requirements
While the tabletop version of HomeView comes with an Apple 30-watt adapter, the wall-mounted version requires you to buy a minimum 20-watt power adapter separately.
What you need to set up HomeView
You must have an iPhone or iPad running the latest version of iOS 27 or iPadOS 27 to set up your new HomeView.
Apps
Out of the box, Apple says that the HomeView comes with the following built-in apps:
- Alarms
- Timers
- World Clock
- Calendar
- FaceTime
- Find My
- Home
- Intercom
- Messages
- Apple Music
- Apple Podcasts
- Reminders
- Safari
- Settings
- Weather
Additionally, Apple mentions that Audiobooks, Apple Music Classical, News, and Apple TV apps will be available from users’ iPhones.
On top of that, the new HomeView will also support third-party audio and video apps.
Spotify, YouTube, Netflix, etc., may support it soon. But don’t take my word for it; Spotify and Netflix still don’t have apps for Vision Pro, and YouTube was reluctant to support visionOS at first.
Siri languages
Siri AI on HomeView is available in English only in the U.S., the UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa, and India.
Accessibility
Apple says the new HomeView supports the following accessibility features:
- VoiceOver
- Screen Zoom
- Voice Control
- Switch Control
- AssistiveTouch
- Real-Time Text
- Live Speech
- Live Captions
- Siri and Dictation
- Type to Siri
- Vocal Shortcuts
- Subtitles and Closed Captioning
Pre-order and availability
- Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, the UK, and the United States: You can pre-order it today (October 13) on Apple’s website.
- Singapore: October 15, at 9 a.m. SGT
- South Africa: Pre-orders can be placed through Apple Authorized Resellers.
HomeView will be available to customers in all the above countries beginning November 13 (Friday).
What about the EU?
At its core, HomeView is a Siri AI-powered device. Because Siri AI isn’t available in the European Union, this new smart hub won’t be available for sale there either. Apple says it is “working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward.”
What do you think of this new smart home device? Will you be buying one?
All images in this post are from Apple.
results.summary:
Apple has launched the HomeView, a $299 smart home hub featuring a 7-inch touchscreen, A18 chip, and facial recognition to provide personalized control for up to six users.

### Key Points
- The device is available in tabletop and wall-mounted versions, both priced at $299, with four color options for the desk model.
- It features a 12MP Center Stage camera for FaceTime, four microphones for Siri, and sensors for temperature, humidity, and ambient light.
- Powered by the Apple A18 chip, the hub supports Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 6.0, and Thread networking for seamless smart home integration.
- Facial recognition allows the device to display personalized information for up to six users across apps like Calendar, Messages, and Reminders.
- Pre-orders begin October 13 in select markets, with a general retail release scheduled for November 13.
- The device is currently unavailable in the European Union due to ongoing regulatory discussions regarding Siri AI availability.

### Why it Matters
The HomeView represents Apple’s strategic push to centralize smart home management through a dedicated, AI-powered interface that bridges the gap between the HomePod and iPad. By integrating personalized facial recognition and the A18 chip, Apple aims to make the device a primary household hub for automation, communication, and media control.

results.title: Not ready to give up Google Assistant? There's apparently a way to bring it back
results.author: sanujb6@gmail.com (Sanuj Bhatia) , Sanuj Bhatia
results.content:
What you need to know
- Google officially replaced Assistant with Gemini in September, but a Redditor has found a way to bring it back.
- The workaround involves uninstalling Google app updates and reopening Google Assistant through the Play Store.
- Users can reportedly decline the Gemini switch and set Google Assistant as their default digital assistant again.
- You'll need to disable automatic Google app updates to keep the workaround working.
A Redditor seems to have found a new trick to get Google Assistant working again on Android phones, even after Google officially shut it down.
Last month, Google pulled the plug on Google Assistant for Android phones on September 4, 2026, replacing the good old assistant with Gemini. Gemini is now the default assistant on Android smartphones, whether you like it or not. However, a new workaround discovered by a Redditor (via Android Police) claims to bring back the Google Assistant experience.
According to the Reddit post, the user managed to get Google Assistant working again by uninstalling updates to the Google app on their Android phone. They then opened the Google Assistant listing on the Play Store, after which the old assistant reportedly started working again.
When Google Assistant launches, a prompt appears asking users to switch to Gemini. But according to the Redditor, there's still an option to decline the switch and continue using Google Assistant instead.
Selecting that option reportedly lets users set Google Assistant as their default digital assistant again, restoring the familiar experience Google discontinued last month. Of course, there's another step you'll need to follow if you want to keep Google Assistant working through this method.
You'll have to disable automatic updates for the Google app on the Play Store. Otherwise, the app could update itself to the latest version and replace Google Assistant with Gemini again. To do this, open the Google Play Store and search for the Google app. Open its listing, tap the three-dot menu in the top-right corner, and uncheck Enable auto-update.
And that's it. If you've been missing the good old Google Assistant experience on your Android phone, this workaround appears to offer a way to bring it back, at least for now.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
Of course, there's no guarantee it'll continue working. Google could disable the workaround through a future update or server-side change at any time. But if you still prefer Google Assistant over Gemini, or simply want to give the old assistant another go for nostalgia's sake, this might be worth trying.>
Sanuj is a tech writer who loves exploring smartphones, tablets, and wearables. He began his journey with a Nokia Lumia and later dived deep into Android and iPhone. He's been writing about tech since 2018, with bylines at Pocketnow, Android Police, Pocket-Lint, and MakeUseOf. When he's not testing gadgets, he's either sipping chai, watching football, or playing cricket.

A Reddit user has discovered a workaround to restore Google Assistant on Android devices by uninstalling recent Google app updates and disabling automatic updates in the Play Store.

### Key Points
- Google officially replaced Google Assistant with Gemini as the default Android digital assistant on September 4, 2026.
- The workaround requires users to uninstall Google app updates and decline the prompt to switch to Gemini upon relaunching the assistant.
- Users must disable automatic updates for the Google app in the Play Store to prevent the system from reverting to Gemini.

This discovery highlights a significant user preference for the legacy Google Assistant experience over the newer Gemini AI integration. It underscores the tension between Google's push for generative AI adoption and the desire of long-term users to maintain familiar, established software functionality on their mobile devices.

results.title: Wikipedians Believed AI Would Come and Go. They Were Wrong
results.author: Richard Cooke
results.content:
Long before the storm of AI struck Wikipedia, the Wikimedia Foundation was making preparations. Wikipedians battened down the hatches and made confident-sounding predictions that it would break and wash over them. Large language models might even improve Wikipedia, it was said, automating more of the housekeeping—formatting, sources, citations, missing links—and so freeing up humans to do creative work. It was not so simple. In 2019, then-Wikimedia Foundation head Katherine Maher wrote an op-ed in The New York Times under the headline “Without Humans, A.I. Can Wreak Havoc.” “Too often,” she wrote, “artificial intelligence is presented as an all-powerful solution to our problems, a scalable replacement for people.” The issue confronting Wikipedia, retaining human control over machines, was the same one soon being faced everywhere.
Already in 2018 Google was training AI to write “Wikipedia-like articles,” and by October 2024, a Princeton University study found that about 5 percent of nearly 3,000 newly created articles on English Wikipedia in a single month (August 2024) contained a substantial amount of AI-generated content. There were signs. ChatGPT was fond of em dashes—parenthetical statements that look like this one—and curly quotation marks. Sometimes, residues from the prompts used to compose articles were left behind (“Here is your Wikipedia article,” they might say.)
At first, Wikipedians tried to shape and control AI, to make its output “acceptable and constructive,” or to fix or remove if it proved otherwise. Generic fluff like “praising a village for its fertile farmlands, livestock, and scenic countryside” and fake sources were weeded out. By March 2026, AI content was found to violate its core principles so often that writing with large language models was banned outright, and their role restricted to translation and minor proofreading.
A much-read essay titled “Death of Wikipedia” explained this defensive posture. It predicted a ripple effect: As contributors reduced their contributions in response to AI pervading the platform, there might be a temptation to replace their work with still more AI, creating a downward spiral. One viral X post lamented that artificial intelligence seemed to be changing things in the wrong direction: “I want AI to do my laundry and dishes so that I can do art and writing, not for AI to do my art and writing so that I can do my laundry and dishes.” The “Death of Wikipedia” warned against something similar: Rather than AI performing Wikipedia’s “housekeeping” roles, it might compose its articles instead, leaving humans relegated to formatting and cleanup. The result would trap editors in an endless curatorial project derived not from human priorities but from the frostbitten harvests of machines.
“The potential ‘whittling down’ each year of our pool of talented writers is the greatest threat to Wikipedia,” another Wikipedian wrote, “as we must increase the number of editors, especially expert editors, to be able to fix the sprawling hellscape of weak, inaccurate and incomplete articles that drag down the project.” A Wikipedia written and read by machines threatened to create a new, deracinated Wikipedia, stripped not only of its context, but of its animating passion. It would be artless, and soulless. When the Wikimedia Foundation says that the care and commitment of Wikipedians to “reliable encyclopedic knowledge is something AI cannot replace,” that is not the same as saying that it will not be replaced.
Once Google introduced AI Overviews in search, they quickly became as central to the experience as Wikipedia was until recently. (This also means Wikipedia still does play a crucial role as a source, only at one step removed.) Anyone who uses AI agents knows that they give plausible, almost intuitive answers, which can pass a superficial review of their sourcing. They are also often wrong. If Wikipedia itself becomes corrupted by artificial intelligence, by what means will we prove when they are wrong?
Implicit in the idea of a single, machine-edited encyclopedia to rule them all is that such a phenomenon should act as a final authority. Its appeal, to the kind of people who find it appealing, is that it will be coolly rational, a kind of digital King Solomon that can act as a disinterested arbiter. There is no reason to think such cold logic would not be cruel instead. Its aesthetic failings are a clue: “Slop” is a useful word for the product of artificial intelligence, which implies something unvariegated and monotonous, absent not only of nutritional value but also of the flavor that makes nutrition a pleasure.
There is also no reason to believe an AI encyclopedia, or any other encyclopedia, should be unifying. Whatever its shortcomings and eccentricities, Wikipedia is the closest thing to an “encyclopedia of everything” we have ever had. Once smartphones became widespread after the iPhone’s launch in 2007, the old speculations, however far-reaching, were realized: Wikipedia was costless, portable, immediate, and electric. Enormous and omnipresent, it really became an approximation of the “sum of all human knowledge.” But so what? What did access to this oracle mean for human flourishing? What good has Wikipedia done?
A documentary maker, wanting to bring Wikipedia’s story to the screen, asked me a sharpened version of this question. Yes, Wikipedia was the little encyclopedia that could. It had overcome humble origins to become massive. But the dictates of streaming television needed something more. Were there, she asked, any real-life episodes where Wikipedia had “saved the village”? Has Wikipedia saved lives? The answer is “probably,” though not in dramatic or famous ways. Quick-fire encyclopedic knowledge has helped with accidental poisoning, and there are signs that Wikipedia is accessed with special frequency during natural disasters. But these anecdotes are difficult to corroborate, and often, when Wikipedia’s role is scrutinized, it turns out to be incidental. If someone calls for help in an emergency, it is not the phone which is the hero.
Does Wikipedia perform a public good? This seems self-evident but is much harder to measure and, in a way, is out of the project’s hands. In 2013, when an online poster posed the question “If someone from the 1950s suddenly appeared today, what would be the most difficult thing to explain to them about life today?” the top answer went viral as a mordant sign of the times: “I possess a device, in my pocket, that is capable of accessing the entirety of information known to man. I use it to look at pictures of cats and get in arguments with strangers.” Elsewhere, the “arguments with strangers” line was expressed in less lighthearted ways. “The greatest threat to democracy may no longer derive from human agency but from new forms of technology, which have the capacity to undermine democracy without anyone having intended it,” the academic David Runciman wrote two years later. “The forces from which democracy needs rescuing are no longer pressing on it from the outside. They come from within.”
No one is credited with foreseeing Wikipedia more clearly than H. G. Wells, a reputation built on a series of essays collected in his book World Brain, and its advocacy for a “Permanent World Encyclopaedia.” But Wells expounded on this idea many times, and his other writings were much more equivocal, and he even satirized his own obsessions in The Camford Visitation: “He wants a universally educated world, educated on the same lines, with every artificial difference eliminated. He is a cantankerous, disagreeable little nobody and yet at times one feels he has got hold of something most exasperatingly vast and right.” Soon after World Brain was published, Wells had lost faith in his encyclopedic vision altogether and succumbed to late-life pessimism. Humanity had orchestrated to create a world war, not a world brain, and in the civilizational race between “education and catastrophe,” as he put it, catastrophe looked to have a winning lead.
Less obvious to us now is that World Brain was also an antidote. The most significant new European encyclopedias that preceded it, the Great Soviet Encyclopedia and the Enciclopedia Italiana, were direct expressions of nationalist and totalitarian intent, so much so that the entry on “Fascism” in the Enciclopedia Italiana was credited to Benito Mussolini himself. Wells understood that “internationalism” needed its own encyclopedia as a counterweight, but that did not make it a simple force for freedom. He assumed that the World Brain would assist a world government in projecting its power, and though democratically available, his Permanent World Encyclopaedia would make such a world government omnipotent. A world government that was all-seeing as well as all-knowing would inevitably be repressive; a sinister side to Wells’ ideas seemed to have partly inspired George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four.
Orwell also critiqued Wells more explicitly in his 1941 essay “Wells, Hitler, and the World State.” One of its more perceptive observations is that Wells was not, in fact, a futurist. He was a nostalgic, Orwell thought, a “nineteenth-century liberal” who had spent 40 years repeating the same idea: that history was a battle between “the man of science who is working towards a planned World State” and “the reactionary who is trying to restore a disorderly past.” With Orwell’s help, we can see that Wells’ World Brain was an old idea, not a new one. Versions of it had preexisted Wells by centuries, and this particular encyclopedic worldview sprang from his Edwardian conception of Progress with a capital P.
The encyclopedia handed down to us from the Enlightenment is much more than a collation of facts in a book or on a website. It is a whole mode of seeing and doing, a lens through which a clear, scientific vision of all things can come into view, unobstructed by superstition. Witness the world in this way, and the world changes. So far-reaching is this idea that the philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre classed “encyclopaedia” as one of the three major approaches of Western ethics, what he called “rival versions of moral enquiry.” The others were “tradition,” starting with Thomas Aquinas and Aristotle, and “genealogy,” which began with Nietzsche. Tradition was a marriage of faith and reason. Genealogy emphasized hidden power relations. Encyclopaedia relied on reason alone, trying to build an objective picture of the world that could determine how to act, thanks to a consensus version of the truth. The purest expression of this was to be found in the 19th century, in the ninth edition of Encyclopaedia Britannica, which promised “the available facts of human history, collected over the widest areas … carefully coordinated and grouped together, in the hope of ultimately evolving the laws of progress, moral and material, which underlie them.”
When Three Rival Versions of Moral Enquiry was published in 1990, MacIntyre’s notion was already criticized for being out of date. One reviewer complained that it saddled “the encyclopaedists with their 19th-century dogmatic statements in Britannica and plays down the fact that few if any of their heirs hold such views today.” Yet there were some places that rational-liberal outlook did survive in an unapologetic form. It remained at the very forefront of Encyclopaedia Britannica—the 1987 edition opened with the motto of its associate, the University of Chicago: “Let knowledge grow from more to more and thus be human life enriched.” Most pertinently, it undergirded the beliefs of Wikipedia’s cofounders. Not only did Wikipedia’s text-heavy format reflect a centuries-old Enlightenment tradition, it was also created by two men who still believed, earnestly, that discovering the facts and learning lessons from them was not only the purpose of an encyclopedia, but the central task of a life well lived.
The divergent paths of Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger offer a kind of parable for the fate of this worldview and the cultural crosscurrents that swamped it. Twenty-five years after Wikipedia’s founding, Wales is still a Davos Man, an international person for an international project, who lives in the capital of the United Kingdom and makes frequent criticism of the MAGA movement. Sanger never left Ohio, where he homeschooled his children, became a vocal vaccine skeptic during the Covid-19 pandemic, and voted for Donald Trump. In 2025, he announced that he had given up his long-standing agnosticism to become a professing Christian, and wrote a book-length philosophical proof for the existence of God. If Wales remained wedded to the MacIntyre-style notion of “encyclopedia”—Enlightenment rationalism, with an added Objectivist trim—Sanger had returned to “tradition.”
As Wikipedia affirmed its status as a knowledge institution, it also lost its immunity from the crises afflicting knowledge institutions everywhere. The only surprise was that it had been exempt for so long. At the end of her tenure as head of the Wikimedia Foundation, Sue Gardner had likened the experience to living on a peaceful tropical island as “cruise missiles flew overhead.” Culture war had broken out all around, and now Wikipedia was an island no more. In the 2010s, “disinformation,” “misinformation,” and “fake news” were all selected as words of the year in short order, and the saturation of information was just as blameworthy as its corruption. Instead of adjudicating between facts like judges, audiences acted like lawyers assembling a brief and took only what they wanted. The results of “doing your own research,” an off-kilter version of the Enlightenment demand “dare to know,” were algorithmically personalized pseudo-informational systems. Mired in this uncertain environment, Wikipedia approached its 25th anniversary facing unprecedented political, cultural, and technological threats.
All of this added an elegiac note to its birthday celebrations in January 2026. The Pew Research company marked the occasion by quantifying the encyclopedia’s staggering reach—in the decade between 2015 and 2025, Wikipedia had been viewed 1.9 trillion times, an average of 508 million views per day. These immense numbers nevertheless contained an unmistakable arc of decline. In the days prior to the anniversary, a long-time Wikipedian, Christophe Henner, published a long and detailed “wake-up call” for the Wikipedia movement. Since 2022, the encyclopedia had lost almost a quarter of its readership, more than 1.1 billion visits per month, a missing audience who, presumably, were seeking out AI summaries instead. Even when answers offered by AI agents contain links, readers tend not to follow them: One figure showed that the click-through rate from AI chatbots was only 0.33 percent; for the Google search engine, it had been closer to 9 percent. For a model whose lifeblood was readers becoming editors, it was a disaster.
Artificial intelligence was an existential risk to Wikipedia, Henner warned, and the encyclopedia risked being remembered as a “historical artifact that AI once trained on … a footnote in the training data of models that have moved on without us.” An editing crisis meant that fewer and fewer editors were performing more and more labor, “a smaller club working harder to maintain something fewer people see,” as he put it. Past moments of opportunity—for example, when Wikipedia might have harnessed the growth of the internet outside Western countries—had mostly been squandered. The energy generated by places like India and Nigeria going digital had passed Wikipedia by, and in the wake of all this, the encyclopedia risked becoming a “temple,” maintained by the last in a priest class of superannuated Wikipedians. Once sacrilegious ideas, like paying editors for their work, had to be considered anew. Otherwise, the whole of Wikipedia might be reduced to an abandoned cathedral.
Media coverage marking the occasion was just as bittersweet. In Nature, Dariusz Jemielniak wrote that “academic indifference” and artificial intelligence threatened Wikipedia’s survival, accusing agentic AI of exploiting a “parasitic relationship” that “endangers the last bastion of freely accessible, human-curated knowledge and undermines the premise of collaboration on which many of Wikipedia’s knowledge-sharing practices rely.” “Wikipedia’s Existential Threats Feel Greater Than Ever” was the headline for a Stephen Harrison piece in WIRED, a catalog of threats beleaguering the project. More dangerous than hostile think tanks and lawmakers was an increasingly indifferent public, slowly drifting away from its founding ideals. “Economic precarity [has] trained many Gen Zers to see any unpaid labor as a scam,” Harrison wrote. In the cold light of the dawning era, becoming a Wikipedia super editor during a period of unemployment seemed a distant luxury, or outright perplexing, “thankless work that AI companies strip-mine for a profit.”
The tide turning on Wikipedia was more than the advent of artificial intelligence or a fragmentation of reading habits. Christophe Henner thought the “AI summaries” were only a “convenient explanation.” “I’m skeptical,” he wrote:
Even this undersold the quantum of change. Something far older was fast losing relevance as well: It was the beginning of the end of the encyclopedic age. Near the front of the French Encyclopédie there is a diagram called the “figurative system of human knowledge,” which is now sometimes called “The Tree of Diderot and d’Alembert.” The Tree is a system for not only ordering “the parts of knowledge,” but connecting them in a logical chain so long it can wreath the universe. It represents a bold idea: that an encyclopedia’s unifying force will show how everything in existence is linked. It suggests that knowing everything will lead to knowing One Big Thing about everything. This old-fashioned idea was resuscitated in the computer age, and gathered momentum with the concept of AGI, artificial general intelligence, the moment machines surpass every form of human understanding. If realized, it will represent not only the end of encyclopedias, but their culmination. Human-written encyclopedias will still exist after AGI, but only as secular scriptures in the mind of a digital god.
The longest-standing critique of “encyclopaedia” is religious: It is the belief that human activity on a godlike scale is a doomed act of conceit. It was only during the Enlightenment that absolute knowledge came to be considered beneficial (and today, “know-it-all” is still an insult, not a compliment). Beforehand, desire for absolute knowledge was viewed as a sin or a crime, a proscription that continues in many cultures. Greek mythology is full of cautionary figures like Pandora and Prometheus, who knew too much and suffered for it; when the Norse god Odin seeks the sacred well waters granting wit and wisdom, a single drink costs him one of his eyes. In the very first book of the Bible, two different stories, the Tower of Babel and the Garden of Eden, carry variations on the same moral: Total understanding must be God’s alone. Curiosity is not only a sin, but the first sin.
One of the many artworks inspired by Wikipedia speaks to this phenomenon. In the 2010s, the bio-artist Joe Davis declared that he would engineer a real, living Tree of Knowledge, the tree described in the Bible that holds forbidden fruit and results in the fall of humankind. To do so, Davis planned to take a 4,000-year-old strain of apple trees and copy the English-language edition of Wikipedia into the letters of its DNA. He called the project Malus ecclesia, which in Latin is a pun that means both “evil church” and “apple tree church.” In interviews, Davis refused to say whether he would eat the Tree’s fruit; because of laws around genetic modification, ingesting an apple or even planning to may have been a criminal act. Mired in red tape, this tantalizing idea never came to fruition, but its forbidding message remains: The sum of all knowledge is cursed.
The real existing Wikipedia feels less melodramatic than that, and the most lasting dividend of Wikipedia may not be its contents but its process, which holds a promise quite unlike the Tree of Knowledge or even the Tree of Diderot. For years, the annual Wikimania conference has sustained a fledgling tradition: At the opening ceremony, Wikipedians wear their national dress. When almost three-quarters of the nations on earth are in attendance, this produces a real spectacle, even against a backdrop of convention center carpet. All around the room are people wearing hanboks and kaftans and kimonos (the practice was initiated by a Japanese Wikipedian), and when they intermingle, the effect is like those old, quaintly hopeful pictures canvassing the “Peoples of the World.” Appreciating the depth and variety on display takes longer. Those golden headdresses, called serimpak, are worn by the seafaring tribes of Borneo, and that is why they are shaped like ships. The chapan robes that seem to swirl under their resplendent colors are from central Asia; those heavy ponchos, overkill against the air-conditioning, have come all the way from the Andes. Someone offers Jimmy Wales a conical nomad’s hat from Burkina Faso, but he cannot accept all the paraphernalia presented to him. There is too much.
Those might be lederhosen in the distance, although someone jokes that the real German national dress is sandals with socks. At least one tech type seems to be wearing Hawaiian shorts for a similar reason, as the official livery of Silicon Valley. Everywhere there is embroidery, silk and brocaded colors, headscarves and skullcaps, a pageant of signs and patterns from parts unknown. Once congregated, the people wearing this garb do not generate an atmosphere of hubris. In this room their shared mission seems humble. Their talk is the slow, uncertain work of mutual understanding, graced with the tentative socializing of the shy. They are bounded by human fallibility, the same thing that ennobles them. Together, they call to mind a Latin phrase very different from Malus ecclesia. E Pluribus Unum—out of many, one.
