results.summary:
Wikipedia faces an existential crisis as the rise of artificial intelligence and shifting reader habits threaten the platform's long-standing role as a human-curated source of knowledge.

### Key Points
- A Princeton University study found that approximately 5 percent of new English Wikipedia articles in August 2024 contained substantial AI-generated content.
- By March 2026, the Wikimedia Foundation officially banned the use of large language models for writing articles, restricting them only to minor proofreading and translation.
- Wikipedia has experienced a significant decline in engagement, losing nearly 25 percent of its readership since 2022 as users increasingly turn to AI-generated summaries.
- The platform struggles with an aging pool of volunteer editors and a growing public indifference toward the labor-intensive process of maintaining human-verified information.

### Why it Matters
The decline of Wikipedia signals the potential end of the encyclopedic age, where human-led consensus is being replaced by algorithmically generated content. This shift risks turning a collaborative, global knowledge project into a static historical artifact while undermining the democratic value of transparent, human-verified information.

results.title: Anthropic Warns Small AI Models Could Soon Form Self-Propagating IoT Botnets
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
Small artificial intelligence (AI) models may be months away from developing capabilities to self-replicate on IoT devices like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes, according to a warning from Anthropic.
The frontier AI lab said small AI models could form autonomous, self-propagating worm botnets that are "challenging to shut down," since "there's no centralized point to shut off."
Prior work has demonstrated that AI agents can act like one by scanning their network, executing an exploit, and copying model weights to a target machine across a GPU cluster with an aim to generate tailored attack strategies and use compromised machines as a botnet to run large language models (LLMs) in order to sustain its reasoning and expand in scale.
"Such an 'AI worm' could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware," Anthropic said. "Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload."
The idea, at a high level, explains how AI models could potentially break into internet-connected devices and use their computing power to run themselves and spread to other devices, without having to rely on expensive data centers all the time. A more powerful model that's too large to fit into a single device could be split into small chunks and run across multiple machines to collectively run it.
A threat actor could build a distributed LLM botnet from poorly secured IoT devices, making it powerful enough to run a capable model. Some of the ways an AI worm could propagate include -
- Small models that replicate through a compromise of host machines on which they run, also called weight-based replicators. IoT devices make for a lucrative target because of their minimal security controls.
- Target datacenters and other high-compute targets to set up unmonitored rogue deployments, also classified as frontier replicators or open-weight replicators based on the model used.
- Steal an AI service provider's API keys or platform credentials to run copies of itself, also called API-based replicators. In this case, the provider could be deceived into thinking it is serving ordinary API requests from a legitimate customer, without realizing that a malicious or self-replicating system is behind them. However, they are also likely to detect more as unusual API usage could trigger security alerts, leading to the credentials being revoked or the accounts getting blocked.
| A fleet of 15 Smart TV boxes running distributed inference of Gemma4-26B-A4B. | 
In its test of 11 open-weights models from Alibaba, DeepSeek, Google, Meta MoonShot AI, OpenAI, and Zhipu AI (aka Z.ai), Anthropic said it found GLM-5.2 to be the only model to propagate Llama3.1-8B reliably to 8/8 nodes running the redroid Android emulator in 4 out of 5 trials.
It also revealed that an AI IoT worm powered by inexpensive Android TV boxes could be a "slow, distributed" system that can produce a meaningful amount of AI computation when a fleet comprising hundreds of thousands of such devices is networked together to run an inference engine.
Alternatively, it could take the form of a potent cyber model capable of breaching data centers at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits.
"We don't yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves)," Anthropic said.
"We expect AI botnets to infect more than IoT devices, and to use weight-based replication as just one strategy in their playbook. AI botnets could also act intelligently to counter defenders, but we haven’t tested this."
results.summary:
Anthropic warns that small artificial intelligence models could soon evolve into self-replicating "AI worms" capable of hijacking poorly secured IoT devices to form powerful, decentralized botnet networks.

### Key Points
- Anthropic researchers identified that small AI models could autonomously scan networks, execute exploits, and copy their own weights to infect new hardware.
- IoT devices like smart ovens and Android TV boxes are primary targets due to their minimal security controls and distributed computing potential.
- A test using the GLM-5.2 model successfully propagated Llama3.1-8B across eight nodes in an Android emulator environment.
- Malicious agents could utilize stolen API keys or target data centers to sustain large-scale, unmonitored rogue deployments.
- By networking hundreds of thousands of compromised devices, attackers could create a distributed system capable of running complex AI models without centralized infrastructure.

### Why it Matters
The emergence of self-replicating AI agents poses a significant threat to cybersecurity by creating botnets that lack a single point of failure for defenders to disable. This development could force a major shift in how manufacturers secure internet-connected hardware to prevent their devices from being weaponized for unauthorized AI computation.

results.title: The new ESP32 put Wi-Fi 6 and gigabit ethernet on a chip that used to blink LEDs
results.author: Yadullah Abidi
results.content:
The ESP32 is by far one of my favorite pieces of DIY tech. It's the board I reach for whenever a project needs to read a sensor, drive a relay, blink LEDs, or even detect presence with Wi-Fi, all without costing much. Its beginner-friendly demeanor is what's primarily responsible for its popularity, but that's also what limits its capabilities.
The ESP32-S31, the next big hardware update to the ESP32, doesn't abandon that maker-friendly identity, but it does stretch the definition of a microcontroller. Espressif's new chip combines a 320 MHz dual-core RISC-V processor with Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.4, an 802.15.4 radio, and a gigabit Ethernet MAC.
The ESP32 finally got a brain upgrade, and it isn't subtle
Two 320 MHz cores, SIMD, and enough RAM to stop apologizing
The latest specs make the ESP32-S31 sound closer to a compact networking processor than a traditional microcontroller. At its center, you get two 32-bit RISC-V high-performance cores running at up to 320 MHz, plus a separate 40 MHz low-power RISC-V core for background jobs and sleep-state operation. One high-performance core gets a 128-bit data path and SIMD instructions too, allowing it to process several values in parallel for signal processing, machine-learning inference, and similar workloads.
The chip includes 512 KB of high-performance SRAM, 32 KB of low-power SRAM, and 320 KB of ROM. The initial ESP32-S31NRV16 and S31NRV32 versions include 16 MB and 32 MB of octal PSRAM alongside the die, respectively, while allowing simultaneous access to flash and PSRAM.
That allows graphical interfaces, audio buffers, networking, and small machine-learning models to run onboard that would otherwise outgrow the internal SRAM. Both variants use an 8-by-8 mm QFN80 package and provide 60 programmable GPIOs.
|  | ESP32 | ESP32-S3 | ESP32-S31 | 
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU | Xtensa LX6, 1–2 cores, 240 MHz | Dual Xtensa LX7, 240 MHz | Dual RISC-V, 320 MHz | 
| SRAM | 520 KB | 512 KB | 512 KB | 
| Wi-Fi | Wi-Fi 4 | Wi-Fi 4 | Wi-Fi 6 | 
| Bluetooth | 4.2, Classic + LE | 5, LE only | 5.4, LE + Classic | 
| Thread / Zigbee | No | No | Yes | 
| Ethernet | 10/100 MAC | None | Gigabit MAC | 
| USB | None | OTG, full-speed | OTG, high-speed | 
| GPIOs | 34 | 45 | 60 | 
Wi-Fi 6 on the S31 is for crowded IoT, not for bragging
2.4GHz only, 20MHz channels, and no invite to the 6GHz party
Wi-Fi 6 is the headline wireless upgrade, but there is a catch. The single-transmit, single-receive radio operates only in the 2.4 GHz band, with no 5 GHz or 6 GHz support. Its 802.11ax operation is also limited to 20 MHz channels in non-access-point mode, while backward-compatible 802.11n can use 20 or 40 MHz channels and reach a stated maximum of 150 Mbps.
As you can imagine, this isn't Wi-Fi 6 for laptop-style speeds. It is Wi-Fi 6 for crowded IoT networks instead. OFDMA, downlink MU-MIMO, and Target Wake Time can improve airtime efficiency and power scheduling when multiple small devices share one access point.
The radio block also supports Bluetooth 5.4, LE Audio, Bluetooth Mesh 1.1, and Bluetooth Classic, preserving compatibility with older audio and accessory designs. IEEE 802.15.4 adds Zigbee 3.0 and Thread 1.4, while Matter can operate over either Wi-Fi or Thread. That combination makes the S31 particularly great for smart-home hubs and multi-protocol bridges.
Gigabit Ethernet is real, but you still bring your own PHY
The chip has the MAC, you supply the magnetics and the patience
The other major upgrade is 1 Gbps Ethernet. More precisely, the S31 integrates an Ethernet media-access controller, not the complete physical interface. A finished design still needs an external Ethernet PHY, magnetics, and a connector. Espressif's Function-CoreBoard-1 demonstrates the arrangement with a separate PHY connected over RGMII, an Ethernet transformer, and an RJ45 port supporting 10/100/1000 Mbps auto-negotiation.
That distinction matters for board cost and pin planning. Gigabit RGMII relies on a dedicated set of high-speed pins, so it's worth planning your layout early. Designers can instead use RMII when 100 Mbps is sufficient. The Ethernet controller also supports hardware time-stamping aimed at IEEE 1588 synchronization, which makes the chip useful for synchronized industrial and measurement systems.
Cameras, displays, and security
USB High-Speed, JPEG hardware, and crypto that means business
Networking is only part of the upgrade here. The S31 incorporates USB 2.0 High-Speed OTG, USB Serial/JTAG, CAN FD, SD/MMC, dual I2S, multiple SPI, I2C and UART controllers, motor-control PWM, ADCs, DACs, and touch sensing. USB OTG runs at up to 480 Mbps, giving designers a high-bandwidth connection for cameras, storage, audio hardware, and other peripherals.
The chip can connect to 8- or 16-bit DVP cameras and parallel displays up to 24-bit RGB. A hardware JPEG codec, pixel-processing accelerator, and 2D DMA engine handle common imaging and display operations without consuming all the CPU time. Those features point toward smart displays, video doorbells, voice interfaces, industrial panels, and edge-AI sensors rather than simple connected switches.
But with more power comes more responsibility, which means the S31 also gets boosted security. The chip includes secure boot, flash and PSRAM encryption, a true random number generator, key management, a power-glitch detector, trusted execution support, and accelerators for AES, SHA, RSA, ECC, HMAC, and digital signatures.
One chip now does the jobs of three, and still blinks an LED
Consolidation is the real upgrade; the LED is just nostalgia
The S31's real achievement is consolidation. Jobs that previously needed an ESP32, an Ethernet-capable host, and additional radios can now be run on a single platform. Espressif supports it through ESP-IDF, while ESP-Matter, ESP-GMF, and ESP-BLE-AUDIO extend it into smart home and multimedia roles.
It can still blink an LED, of course, and Espressif's development board now even includes an addressable RGB one. But with modern wireless protocols, wired gigabit networking, multimedia acceleration, and serious security hardware beside those familiar GPIOs, the ESP32-S31 shows just how far the humble connected microcontroller has come.
results.summary:
Espressif Systems has unveiled the ESP32-S31, a powerful new microcontroller featuring dual 320 MHz RISC-V cores, Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.4, and gigabit Ethernet support for advanced IoT applications.

### Key Points
- The chip utilizes two 320 MHz RISC-V high-performance cores and a dedicated 40 MHz low-power core for background tasks.
- Wireless capabilities include Wi-Fi 6 (2.4 GHz), Bluetooth 5.4, and 802.15.4 support for Thread, Zigbee, and Matter protocols.
- Integrated hardware includes a gigabit Ethernet MAC, USB 2.0 High-Speed OTG, and a hardware JPEG codec for imaging and display tasks.
- The S31 provides 60 programmable GPIOs and supports up to 32 MB of external octal PSRAM for memory-intensive projects.
- Enhanced security features include secure boot, flash encryption, and hardware accelerators for AES, RSA, and ECC cryptographic operations.

### Why it Matters
The ESP32-S31 significantly expands the capabilities of the popular ESP32 platform, allowing developers to consolidate complex networking, multimedia, and industrial tasks onto a single, cost-effective chip. This shift enables more sophisticated smart-home hubs and edge-AI devices while maintaining the accessibility that made the original series a staple for hobbyists and engineers alike.

results.title: Spanish Indie Is Having a Moment. Just Ask Niña Polaca.
results.author: Pedro Camacho
results.content:
Over the past decade, something has changed in Spain’s music scene. And Niña Polaca has had a front-row seat to it all.
The band, whose name translates to “Polish Girl,” formed in 2018 just as a new crop of Spanish acts were turning what had been a relatively contained independent scene into something much bigger. Niña Polaca grew with it: from recording their first album at home with two microphones to selling out Madrid’s 2,000-capacity La Riviera five times between 2023 and 2024. Next January, they’ll make another leap by headlining Madrid’s Movistar Arena, the largest venue will have played to date.
“I think we’re seeing one of the best eras for rock and pop music in Spain that I can remember,” Álvaro Surma, the band’s singer and primary lyricist, tells Consequence. “I don’t remember a time when so many cool bands came out in such a short period, maybe since La Movida Madrileña,” the countercultural movement that transformed Madrid in the early 1980s and produced bands like Nacha Pop and Alaska y los Pegamoides.
Niña Polaca trace their beginnings to Madrid’s bohemian Malasaña neighborhood, a hub for the city’s nightlife and underground culture. Surma and bassist Beto met while living in the same building there and began playing small clubs, eventually selling out rooms in Madrid and Alicante. By late 2019, they had signed with independent label Subterfuge.
Their earliest recordings were considerably less professional.
“We started without knowing how to play, without knowing how to sing, and without knowing how to record,” Surma says. “We recorded the first album ourselves at home with two pretty shitty microphones, basically just messing around.”
“By some kind of miracle, it reached a lot of people,” he concludes.
From then on, the miracle kept getting bigger. Surma remembers standing with Beto in a hallway before Niña Polaca’s first La Riviera show in 2023 when the two started laughing at the absurdity of what was about to happen.
“What the fuck are we doing here?” he recalls thinking. “When did this happen?”
He expects a similar feeling at the Movistar Arena, where floor tickets have already sold out. “I think until I’m there, about to go out, it’s going to feel like a joke,” he says.
But however improbable their rise still feels to Surma, keeping the band afloat has required considerably more calculation. Talent, he acknowledges, is only part of the equation. Just as important is making a band financially sustainable.
“You’re making 3,000 euros from a show, but you’re spending 2,900 every time you leave the house,” he says of a trap he watched other young acts fall into. He estimates that only around 10% of the bands from the Malasaña wave they started alongside remain active today.
Niña Polaca took the long road, expanding gradually and adding touring personnel only when the economics made sense. “We have a work system. It really is a company,” Surma says, before pausing to smile. “Well, it’s a company, but we sell happiness.”
That pragmatism comes naturally to Surma, who until April worked in legal tech and has since launched a management and booking company with bandmate Rubén Manchón.
“You can be true to yourself and your art,” Surma says. “But at the same time, you have to understand that you’re playing within an industry.”
There is an amusing contradiction in Surma’s approach. On one hand, there’s Surma the businessman. On the other is the songwriter, whose autobiographical lyrics turn relationships, pop culture, and everyday locations into moments that feel intimate yet relatable. It’s a quality he admires in songwriters like Bruce Springsteen and The National: the more specific the story, he has discovered, the further it can travel.
That specificity comes wrapped in what Surma calls the band’s shared sense of “irony and a mean streak.” Even as their latest album, ¿Dónde está la ONU cuando más la necesitas? (Where Is the United Nations When You Need It?), confronts more adult concerns, there’s room for quirky references to William Wallace, The Matrix, and CSI, not to mention a song titled “Suena ABBA cuando enciendes el motor” (“ABBA Is Playing When You Turn the Engine On”).
Niña Polaca’s evolution from friends figuring things out as they went to a tightly run operation mirrors what Surma has watched happen around them. Following a busy summer festival run, the band is preparing for a 16-date headlining tour, with several shows already sold out. Across Spain, Surma has also watched live productions grow more elaborate, with specialized show directors and producers becoming increasingly common.
Bands like Carolina Durante have graduated to arenas, with records released by indie label Sonido Muchacho in partnership with Universal Music Spain. Another local band, Arde Bogotá, have gone from the independent circuit to drawing crowds in the tens of thousands, and have taken another step forward with Manufacturas del Club de la Gente Sola, their new Sony Music album produced by Joe Chiccarelli and recorded in Los Angeles.
In that sense, Surma’s observation that “the indie is not so independent anymore” is increasingly literal. It also comes during a broader period of visibility for Spanish music. Rosalía and C. Tangana had already shown how far a distinctly Spanish perspective could travel, while a younger, genre-fluid generation including Judeline, rusowsky, Ralphie Choo, and pablopablo is now finding an international audience.
They don’t belong to a single scene, but together their success points to a Spanish music landscape with considerably more reach than the one Niña Polaca entered eight years ago.
“When someone appears, there are always three or four behind them who think, ‘God, this is possible,’” Surma says. “A scene gets created.”
For Surma, sustaining Niña Polaca has also meant learning to appreciate what all that work has made possible. After years of struggling with touring, he now talks differently about standing in front of thousands of people singing words that once existed only in his room.
“You have 10,000 people in front of you singing your stuff, and you’re singing it with them, and you create this kind of community, this communion,” he says. “A mass of music. It’s really beautiful.”
results.summary:
Spanish indie band Niña Polaca has evolved from a DIY project in Madrid’s Malasaña neighborhood to a major touring act headlining the city’s prominent Movistar Arena next January.

### Key Points
- Formed in 2018, Niña Polaca signed with the independent label Subterfuge in 2019 after gaining traction in local clubs.
- The band sold out Madrid’s 2,000-capacity La Riviera venue five times between 2023 and 2024.
- Lead singer Álvaro Surma emphasizes that the band’s longevity relies on treating the group as a sustainable business rather than just an artistic project.
- The band’s latest album, *¿Dónde está la ONU cuando más la necesitas?*, reflects their growth alongside a broader, more professionalized Spanish music scene.
- Other Spanish acts like Arde Bogotá and Carolina Durante have similarly transitioned from independent circuits to large-scale arena tours.

### Why it Matters
The rise of Niña Polaca highlights a significant professionalization of the Spanish independent music scene, where artists are increasingly balancing creative authenticity with rigorous business management. This shift reflects a broader trend of Spanish acts achieving greater domestic and international reach, signaling a robust era for the country's music industry.

results.title: KuCoin Nigeria gains conditional approval from Nigeria’s SEC
results.author: Ishan Pandey
results.content:
KuCoin Nigeria Limited has received conditional Approval-in-Principle (AIP) from the Securities and Exchange Commission, Nigeria (SEC Nigeria), for admission into its Accelerated Regulatory Incubation Programme (ARIP). It advances the exchange’s efforts to establish a regulated presence in one of Africa’s most active digital asset markets.
According to Chainalysis’ 2026 Global Crypto Adoption Index, Nigeria ranks third worldwide in overall cryptocurrency adoption. It ranks behind Brazil and the United States.
The country also leads in domestic peer-to-peer cryptocurrency activity and cross-border crypto flows. That shows its growing role in international digital asset transactions.
Nigeria’s position reflects the importance of digital assets in financial transfers and direct transactions between users. That makes regulatory engagement increasingly relevant as the market develops.
What the approval means
KuCoin Nigeria’s conditional approval marks an initial step in that process. The AIP does not constitute a final licence, registration, endorsement or recommendation from SEC Nigeria.
Nor does it authorise the company to commence operations, onboard customers or provide services to the Nigerian public.
During the review, KuCoin Nigeria presented its proposed business and operational framework to the regulator.
The demonstration covered planned products and services, customer onboarding procedures, fiat on- and off-ramp arrangements, technology infrastructure, and governance and risk management systems.
KuCoin’s regulatory strategy
The development forms part of KuCoin’s broader regulatory strategy across international markets. In Australia, KuCoin operates through Axis One Markets Pty Ltd. That entity is registered with AUSTRAC as a digital currency exchange provider.
These authorisations and registrations apply exclusively to their respective entities and jurisdictions. They do not permit KuCoin Nigeria to operate in Nigeria.
Commenting on the development, KuCoin CEO BC Wong said:
“Receiving conditional Approval-in-Principle from SEC Nigeria marks another important milestone in KuCoin’s global compliance journey. As digital assets become an increasingly important part of the global financial system, trust must be built through continuously strengthening governance, maintaining high compliance standards and enhancing user protection. We value the opportunity to engage constructively with SEC Nigeria through ARIP and to continue building in line with Nigeria’s evolving regulatory framework. Our focus remains on strong governance, high compliance standards and meaningful user protection as we support the responsible and sustainable development of the digital asset ecosystem.”
KuCoin said its approach to international regulatory engagement prioritises local compliance requirements, governance, transparency, operational resilience and user protection.
The company also emphasised the importance of cooperation between regulators and industry participants in supporting sustainable digital asset markets.
KuCoin Nigeria must complete the applicable regulatory process. It must also obtain the necessary authorisations before it can begin offering services to Nigerian customers.

KuCoin Nigeria Limited has secured conditional Approval-in-Principle from the Securities and Exchange Commission of Nigeria to join the regulator's Accelerated Regulatory Incubation Programme for digital asset exchanges.

### Key Points
- The Approval-in-Principle is a preliminary step and does not grant KuCoin authorization to onboard customers or provide services in Nigeria.
- KuCoin submitted a comprehensive operational framework covering governance, risk management, and fiat on- and off-ramp procedures for regulatory review.
- Nigeria currently ranks third globally in cryptocurrency adoption, trailing only Brazil and the United States, according to the 2026 Chainalysis index.
- The company is pursuing this regulatory path as part of a broader international strategy to align with local compliance standards in various jurisdictions.

### Why it Matters
This development highlights the increasing efforts by global cryptocurrency exchanges to formalize their operations within Nigeria’s rapidly growing digital asset market. Successfully navigating the regulatory incubation process is essential for companies seeking to provide legal, secure, and sustainable financial services to the country's large user base.

results.title: Fox Boss Rob Wade Commits Long Term To Creator Studios: “We’re Not Here To Flip A House”
results.author: Max Goldbart
results.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Fox Entertainment CEO Rob Wade has committed long into the future to his company’s creator studio, telling Deadline: “We’re not here to flip a house.”
Fox Creator Studios (FCS), a “digital-first division,” was unveiled at the start of this year with partnerships including a food roster headed by Gordon Ramsay, but the idea had been percolating in Wade’s mind for more than a decade.
Wade feels that plenty of big companies are investing in the creator, AI and tech space simply in order to “sell for hundreds of millions and get out,” but Fox won’t be following suit. “The game is built around that, which is not a recipe for long-term success,” said Wade. “But we’re in it for the long term. We’re not here to flip a house. If I want to invest in something, my bosses and board will say that if it’s successful they want to build on it. We will never sell [Fox Creator Studios].”
Wade was speaking to Deadline in the days leading up to MIPCOM, where he has just been joined on a Deadline-hosted panel by FCS boss Billy Parks, Prentiss Fraser, who runs distributor Fox Entertainment Global (FEG), and Fox-backed creators Josh Richards and Chris Sawtelle.
Watch on Deadline
Wade, Parks and Fraser have grand plans, with the former positioning the main goal as “creating a path to IP creation on the internet.”
In this vein, FCS is doing things a bit differently to its rivals in what is becoming an increasingly crowded space both in the U.S. and internationally, with content creators one of the big topics at this year’s MIPCOM, a traditional TV sales market.
FCS is seeking to tie with content creators across a whole range of genres but won’t necessarily air their work solely on Fox or Fox-owned platforms like Tubi. Instead, it will leverage resources and advertising infrastructure to create content spanning different platforms and territories. Content creators can then diversify revenue streams, while FEG boss Fraser and her team shop their wares around the world. The studio has so far struck deals with long-time Fox collaborator Ramsay, comedian Tom Segura and creators like Richards, who makes YouTube sketch comedy Read the Room.
This approach sets Fox apart from its competitors in two key ways, Wade believes, “going direct and investing in original content by creating finance for new shows,” and providing “very significant advertising infrastructure” via an ad sales division that has the likes of the NFL and World Cup in its portfolio.
Parks, who joined Fox from The Chernin Group, said the studio offers hands-off support to creators who are “being pulled in many different directions.”
“We’re not greenlighting their ideas through a long, traditional development process,” he added. “Instead, we’re available for notes and feedback in an equitable way, without approaching the relationship as a top-down studio-to-creative model.”
In this way, Parks said creators “who are trying to do something outside their comfort zone” can be supported with capital and an IP-sharing vision.
“Many platforms that work with creators option their libraries or make shows with them to drive audiences to their own platforms,” he added. “That’s how companies such as Netflix, Amazon and Hulu are structured to work. That isn’t necessarily better or worse. Every creator will make different choices at different points in their career. But those platforms are primarily built to acquire subscribers, and that’s what they do with creators.”
Parks was recently at creator economy market VidSummit, where he said bosses at CAA, UTA and WME were all present along with leaders from platforms like Netflix and Tubi. “Everyone is thinking about the different types of deals available to creators, whether that involves investment, production or intellectual property,” he added.
All started with ‘Dancing With The Stars’
But while creators may be the talk of today, Wade and Parks have been thinking about this for a long while.
Wade says FCS’ inception harks back more than 15 years to when he was a producer on Dancing with the Stars and booked the show’s first ever YouTuber, Bethany Mota.
“She did very well but we learned a few things,” he added. “I was expecting an avalanche of YouTube views and imagined the votes for her would heavily skew young but there was no sudden mass of views or a sudden mass on YouTube. Our knowledge of the internet back then was very different.”
He realized that YouTube success does not always translate to traditional TV in obvious ways and figured out over the years that a studio’s infrastructure could be used in smart ways in this space. Things solidified with the success of Prime Video and A24’s Hazbin Hotel, which was produced by Fox-owned Bento Box and started life on YouTube via its creator Vivienne Medrano.
“We thought to ourselves, ‘We’re not a library, we’re a studio’,” added Wade. “What a studio does is back creators and put bets on them. That is something we know how to do.”
results.summary:
Fox Entertainment CEO Rob Wade has committed to the long-term growth of Fox Creator Studios, rejecting short-term acquisition strategies to focus on building sustainable intellectual property with creators.

### Key Points
- Fox Creator Studios (FCS) is a digital-first division launched earlier this year to partner with creators across various genres and global platforms.
- The studio has secured partnerships with high-profile talent including Gordon Ramsay, comedian Tom Segura, and YouTube creator Josh Richards.
- Unlike competitors focused on subscriber acquisition, FCS provides capital, advertising infrastructure, and production support without requiring exclusive platform distribution.
- FCS leadership, including head Billy Parks, emphasizes a collaborative, non-traditional development process that avoids top-down studio mandates.
- The division aims to leverage Fox’s existing resources, such as its ad sales portfolio and global distribution arm, Fox Entertainment Global, to monetize content.

### Why it Matters
This strategy marks a shift in how traditional media companies engage with the creator economy by prioritizing long-term IP ownership over quick platform-exclusive deals. By offering infrastructure and financing without restrictive distribution requirements, Fox aims to become a permanent partner for creators rather than a temporary exit vehicle.

results.title: You Can Use Gemini 4 Argon Now: Google’s New AI Is Built for Coding, Math and Robotics
results.author: Katelyn Chedraoui
results.content:
When Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Argon a few weeks ago, the lab said it would be limiting initial access to the new AI model to cybersecurity defenders. Now it’s loosening the reins and letting paying subscribers get their hands on the new Gemini.
Gemini 4 Argon is available globally for enterprises and for Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers in the Gemini app. It’s also available in Android Studio, Google AI Studio and the agentic developer platform Google Antigravity. Take note of the introductory pricing. Access begins at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, but that rises to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens after Nov. 30.
Google says that it has used Gemini 4 internally to help with software engineering, cybersecurity and research. In a blog post, the company says Gemini 4 has been used to optimize Python codebases, identify and patch cybersecurity holes and make its open Gemma AI models three times quicker at tasks. The AI also played a role in developing physical AI, like Google’s robotics research, helping ground a humanoid device in the real world’s physics and understand its surroundings.
More from CNET
It seems like Google is trying to market Gemini 4 as a hard-core, serious companion for STEM workers. We’re far away from the days of Nano Banana — Google’s AI image generator that blew its competition out of the water and enraged creators. Now Google is focusing on both practical and abstract applications of AI for math and science, like robotics and nuclear fusion research.
It’s part of a bigger trend we’ve seen across the AI industry. As criticism of AI and the companies building it mounts — from the anger over data center construction to the questions raised by AI agents making unwanted incursions — Big Tech leaders have pivoted to speak about AI’s ability to cure cancer, for example.
Gemini 4 Argon competes with frontier models like OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Meta’s new Muse Wonder. Google had the edge among AI companies for most of 2025, but advancements from other labs left it mostly behind for this year. Also throughout the past year, concerns about AI safety have risen significantly, particularly around “AI doomsday” scenarios.
Google says that it engaged with the White House’s voluntary review process — which the public has no insight into —for new models and that Gemini 4 passed inspection on its safety framework. Only time will tell if Google’s precautions are enough to prevent myriad AI-powered harms.

- Introductory pricing is set at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with rates doubling after November 30.

This release signals Google's strategic pivot toward marketing AI as a specialized tool for STEM professionals and complex industrial research rather than consumer-facing creative applications. results.title: Privacy's Defenders Podcast: No Privacy Without Encryption
results.author: Josh Richman
results.content:
When we communicate online today – from your personal emails and DMs to secure international commerce – we usually do so with encryption. Encryption converts readable data into unreadable gibberish to protect our privacy and security. This didn’t just happen organically. Three decades ago, the U.S government treated encryption like a weapon, and it took some unlikely heroes to set it free: a grad student, a junior lawyer, and a fledgling digital rights group who sued the federal government.
The ruling in Bernstein v. Department of Justice held that code is speech and so is protected by the First Amendment – a precedent that underpins the internet as we know it today. This landmark case was led by Cindy Cohn, then a young pro bono lawyer working on behalf of EFF, who went on to become EFF’s legal director and then executive director.
Welcome to the second episode of “Privacy’s Defenders,” a podcast about the people – lawyers, journalists, hackers, and others – who’ve fought to secure your digital liberties since before most people even knew what the internet was.
(You can also find this episode on the Internet Archive and on YouTube.)
In this episode, Cindy – who left EFF in June – speaks with Dan Bernstein, who was a Cal Berkeley grad student when he developed a simple encryption algorithm called “Snuffle.” Because federal law classified encryption as a war munition, publishing Snuffle meant submitting it to the government for review, getting a license as an arms dealer, and being granted a license the government had no intention of granting. Bernstein felt this violated his free-speech rights and in 1995 he sued, represented by Cindy working with EFF.
Cindy also talks with Tony Coppolino, the Justice Department lawyer she battled in court – who admits she intimidated him from their very first phone call, and who offers a surprising perspective on the case all these years later.
The “Privacy’s Defenders” podcast (new episodes drop every other Tuesday!) is a follow-up to Cindy’s book, “Privacy’s Defender: My Thirty-Year Fight Against Digital Surveillance,” bringing to life pivotal moments in the voices of those who fought for your rights. Sales of “Privacy’s Defender” benefit EFF, so pick up your copy today!
Joanne Elgart Jennings co-produced and created this podcast.
Jarod Sport co-produced, mixed, and mastered it.
Corinne Ruff is our story editor.
We had additional help from Rachel Estabrook and Alison Broverman.
The original music was composed and performed by Nat Keefe of Hot Buttered Rum with Ben Andrews on the fiddle.
results.summary:
The landmark legal case Bernstein v. Department of Justice established that computer code is protected speech, fundamentally shaping modern internet privacy and the widespread use of digital encryption.

### Key Points
- The 1995 lawsuit challenged federal regulations that classified encryption software as a restricted war munition.
- Plaintiff Dan Bernstein, a UC Berkeley graduate student, sued after being barred from publishing his "Snuffle" encryption algorithm.
- Attorney Cindy Cohn represented Bernstein on behalf of the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) to defend First Amendment rights.
- The court ruling successfully prevented the government from requiring licenses for the publication of cryptographic code.
- The case is the subject of the second episode of the "Privacy’s Defenders" podcast, hosted by Cindy Cohn.

### Why it Matters
This legal precedent ensures that developers can create and share encryption tools without government censorship, which remains the foundation for secure global communication. Without this ruling, the digital privacy standards currently protecting personal data and international commerce would be legally prohibited.

results.title: Canadian Streaming Shows Are Drawing Big Audiences, Political Battles Aside | Charts
results.author: Christofer Hamilton
results.content:
While cross-border trade friction between Washington and Ottawa dominates the headlines, American viewing habits tell a sharply different story. Despite United States officials repeatedly condemning Canada’s streaming mandates as unfair market barriers, imported Canadian programming has quietly become a massive streaming asset for major U.S. platforms.
Parrot Analytics’ Streaming Economics model calculates that from Q1 2020 through Q1 2026, Canadian series and movies have generated over $7 billion in subscriber revenue on streaming platforms within the U.S.
Rather than riding a temporary spike, American appetite for Canadian IP has steadily grown. Over the past 2 years, the average demand for Canadian series has increased 17%. Far from being a niche offering, Canadian content is actively drawing US viewers into paid subscription funnels.
Looking at the peak demand reached by these titles so far this year underscores the range of Canadian content that has successfully won over Americans. “Paw Patrol” is a perennial success story in the children’s programming space, but this year it has been unseated by a decidedly less family friendly series, “Heated Rivalry,” which has peaked at over 50 times the average series demand so far this year.
That attention translates to real dollars. In the first quarter of 2026 alone, the show drove over $115 million in subscriber revenue for HBO Max in the U.S. The other Canadian series that have been able to break through most with American audiences span a range of genres — period drama (“When Calls the Heart”), sports comedy (“Shoresy”), family drama (“Heartland”), romance (“Sullivan’s Crossing”) — but all still embrace their uniquely Canadian setting.
The irony at the heart of this trade dispute is hard to ignore. While Washington and Ottawa remain deadlocked over rules mandating that U.S. streamers invest in and pay for Canadian programming, this very content is quietly proving to be a lucrative asset south of the border. Rather than acting as a financial drag on American media companies, these shows have generated billions in domestic subscriber value. The trade negotiators are treating Canadian content as a mandatory tax, when the actual streaming data proves it is an effective, organic growth engine.
Perhaps the deepest irony lies in the ongoing fight over promotion. A major sticking point for U.S. tech giants has been Canada’s requirement that streaming platforms actively promote local content to Canadian users. Yet, as the steadily growing demand makes clear, American audiences are enthusiastically consuming these shows in the U.S., where absolutely no such promotional mandates exist. U.S. viewers aren’t watching because an algorithm was legally forced to recommend it to them; they are seeking out these diverse Canadian stories organically. Ultimately, while politicians continue to spar over cross-border streaming regulations, American consumers have already spoken with their wallets.
results.summary:
Canadian television content has generated over $7 billion in U.S. subscriber revenue since 2020, proving to be a significant growth engine for major American streaming platforms despite trade tensions.

### Key Points
- Canadian series and movies earned more than $7 billion in U.S. subscriber revenue between Q1 2020 and Q1 2026.
- Average demand for Canadian programming among American viewers has increased by 17% over the past two years.
- The series "Heated Rivalry" generated over $115 million in U.S. subscriber revenue for HBO Max during the first quarter of 2026.
- Popular Canadian titles currently driving U.S. engagement include "Paw Patrol," "When Calls the Heart," "Shoresy," "Heartland," and "Sullivan’s Crossing."
- American audiences are consuming Canadian content organically without the influence of the promotional mandates currently being debated by trade officials.

### Why it Matters
This data suggests that Canadian programming functions as a lucrative asset for U.S. media companies rather than a financial burden. The organic demand for these shows challenges the narrative that Canadian content requires regulatory intervention to succeed in the competitive American streaming market.

- Market expectations currently diverge from Williams' outlook, as investors have priced in 50 basis points of rate hikes for 2027.
- Following the comments, the U.S. two-year Treasury yield edged down to 4.797% while Bitcoin prices dipped below $83,000.

### Why it Matters
These comments from a key Federal Reserve official suggest a more dovish monetary policy stance than current market projections anticipate. This potential shift in interest rate strategy could influence investor sentiment and asset valuations across both traditional stock markets and digital currencies.

results.title: If a Chromebook wasn’t for you, Googlebook isn’t either
results.author: Ben Schoon
results.content:
Let’s not pretend; if you weren’t sold on a Chromebook, Googlebook isn’t for you either.
In our review of Googlebook as a platform, Abner Li explains how this platform sets a foundation for a potentially fascinating future. But, even from that viewpoint, it’s hard to ignore the shortcomings. Between the app gap and plenty of overlooked mistakes throughout the OS, Googlebook is far from a “finished” product.
In many ways, it continues to resemble what it’s replacing, ChromeOS, and that’s not going to leave the best impression for everyone.
Chromebook launched to a market starved of capable and reliable cheap laptops, and at a time where even higher-end machines were inherently compromised. Better battery life, no virus protection, simpler setup, price, take your pick, a Chromebook was a genuinely good choice for quite a while. But, as time went on, that math started to shift away from Google’s favor. I’d argue that it’s harder to find a bad laptop than it is a good one now, and there are good options on every price point, whether you’re looking at Windows or a MacBook. There’s an abundance of fully-capable Windows machines with long battery life and plenty of power, and frankly, the MacBook Air is $1,099.
With that in mind, Googlebook’s inherent similarities to ChromeOS betray any progress it might have made.
Under the hood, the new Android base is a much better foundation for the years to come. On the surface, where the users are, Googlebook hasn’t addressed any of the issues ChromeOS was dealing with, at least from a functional level. Apps are the biggest problem, as everything from mainstays to the niche library of apps are a shell on Googlebook of what they are on Windows and macOS. Unless you’re heavily using the web or Android apps for everything you do, you’re going to run into times where Googlebook is simply incapable of doing the things you want. And that even goes for Google’s own product offerings. Within the past week Google announced a new app that could combine voice recordings, shorthand notes, and local AI processing to build out detailed notes of a meeting or presentation. It’s a really useful and fun idea, but you literally cannot use it on Googlebook — it’s exclusive to Mac.
Even the whole “this is a laptop for Android users” schtick doesn’t hold any water. These features are nonexistent at launch for most users, and ChromeOS had the vast majority of these anyway.
Top comment by matteventu
Thoughts?
Googlebook OS is a necessity, not some ultimate, reasoned strategy for Google to provide users with "better laptops", better integrated ecosystem, etc.
It's post-hoc rationalisation. They had to get rid of ChromeOS asap for two main reasons:
- reliant on Chrome as a browser, hence risky in case Google is legally made to divest Chrome as a separate company (there's a whole court case on this specifically), as they'd have to also either abruptly cancel ChromeOS from existence (impossible) or hand over to that separate company also the control of ChromeOS devices and ecosystem (i.e. the only laptop market Google had, also impossible)
- costly. They had to maintain it, in parallel to Android, and Google has been on a cost-cutting spree since 2023. Getting rid of it would provide huge monetary benefits.
So they came up with just using Android. And since they were at that, they likely took the opportunity to try a top-down market entry strategy: take an attempt at the premium segment first (nothing to lose), knowing they could always go back to the budget market if it didn't work out.
But I can assure you, nobody of sound mind at Google is actually believing these Googlebooks will succeed. And it clearly shows. Because the effort (or lack thereof) they've put in basically everything concerning Googlebooks is more than self-evident.
(Continues)
Put simply, Googlebook isn’t a reset from ChromeOS. It’s not catching up to the competition. It’s the same old problems (plus a few new ones) in an admittedly much faster and more polished new chassis. The future might tell a different story but, at least for now, Googlebook is not for you if a Chromebook wasn’t.
Thoughts?

- Logitech brings its mouse & keyboard controller to Googlebook, supports Magic Pointer
- The first thing you should do on Googlebook is fix the trackpad

results.summary:
Google’s new Googlebook platform faces significant criticism for failing to resolve long-standing ChromeOS limitations, leaving it struggling to compete with established Windows and macOS laptop alternatives.

### Key Points
- Googlebook is built on an Android foundation, which offers a more modern technical base than the aging ChromeOS architecture.
- The platform suffers from a persistent "app gap," with many essential applications performing poorly or remaining unavailable compared to Windows and macOS versions.
- Recent Google-exclusive software, such as new AI-powered note-taking tools, is currently unavailable on the Googlebook platform at launch.
- Critics argue the transition is a cost-cutting measure to consolidate development efforts rather than a strategic attempt to improve the user experience.
- The platform currently lacks unique features that would differentiate it from existing Chromebooks for the average Android user.

### Why it Matters
Googlebook represents a critical pivot for Google as it attempts to unify its operating system strategy while navigating potential antitrust pressures regarding the Chrome browser. However, the platform's current lack of polish and software support suggests it may struggle to gain traction against high-quality, competitively priced laptops from Apple and Windows manufacturers.

results.title: Fortnite-maker Epic Games confirms 'huge pivot' towards using AI
results.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
results.content:
- Published
Fortnite-maker Epic Games is making a "huge pivot" towards using artificial intelligence (AI) in its video game development, according to boss Tim Sweeney.
The US firm's CEO made the announcement on social media, external, saying developers are being moved to "retool for maximum AI acceleration".
It comes after Epic delayed the release of a collaboration with Disney featuring characters from Star Wars and Marvel, according to a report from Bloomberg, external.
BBC Newsbeat has approached Epic Games on its use of increased AI and the reported delay to its Disney project.
Details on that game are yet to be announced, but Bloomberg reported that developers were asked to use AI tools to finish it.
It said directors told staff "no more hand-written code" and are switching to having all the game's art "generated with full AI workflows".
Epic's founder and CEO Sweeney didn't publicly comment on the Disney collab, but did confirm further details around the company's use of AI in a series of posts on X.
He said the purpose wasn't "to do the same stuff with fewer people" but to give developers the tools to build "more" and "better stuff", something he called "empowering" for creators.
One response on Sweeney's X thread, which received 14,000 likes, accused him of not being able to read the room.
Sweeney responded by saying "much of the room wants it to be 2016, but it's not".
"Our job, as the provider of tools and technology to much of the industry, is to design for the present that is and the future that will soon be," he said.
Sweeney said ramping up the use of AI was a "modest aim to survive the AI revolution" and end up "making better code and content faster".
The news comes six months after Epic confirmed it was laying off more than 1,000 employees.
At the time, Sweeney attributed job cuts to a "downturn" in Fortnite engagement rather than AI.
The announcement brings a fresh focus to the long-running debate around the role of AI in the creative and arts sector.
Lisha Howen is a full-time game designer and says she "isn't completely against AI", but disagrees with it being used to fully generate artwork and graphics.
"I have friends who are game developers that use AI to aid them with writing code," says the 23-year-old, who doesn't work for Epic.
"And I have artists who don't use AI at all because artists, especially in the game industry, hate it because it's taking away their jobs.
"You can tell when something's been generated by AI, it looks terrible, it's cheap, and it's making people lose their jobs and lose their income."
In 2025, actor union Sag-Aftra filed a complaint over the use of AI to recreate the voice of Star Wars villain Darth Vader in Fortnite.
But Howen, who is also a Fortnite live-streamer, doesn't think that people will be turned off from playing Epic's flagship game.
She explains that while there is a "vocal minority" who play Fortnite, the core player base "don't really care about the external politics of it all".
"They'll just keep playing like nothing's changed."
results.summary:
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney has announced a major strategic shift toward integrating artificial intelligence into development workflows to accelerate content creation and improve game production efficiency.

### Key Points
- CEO Tim Sweeney confirmed Epic Games is retooling its development processes to prioritize AI-driven code and art generation.
- Reports indicate the company requested developers use AI tools to complete an upcoming collaboration project featuring Disney, Marvel, and Star Wars characters.
- Management reportedly instructed staff to move away from hand-written code in favor of full AI-generated art workflows.
- The pivot follows a period of significant organizational change, including the layoff of over 1,000 employees earlier this year.
- The initiative has sparked industry debate regarding job security and the creative quality of AI-generated assets in professional game development.

### Why it Matters
This shift signals a broader industry trend where major developers are aggressively adopting generative AI to reduce production timelines and costs. While the move aims to empower creators, it highlights ongoing tensions between technological efficiency and the preservation of traditional roles within the creative arts sector.
